## cabinet new

```sh
cabinet new [dir] [options]
```

Creates a workspace in an empty or missing folder. In a terminal it asks a question for each setting; options set the defaults, and `--yes` skips the questions.

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `[dir]` | asked (`~/dev/<name>`) | Must not exist, or be empty. |
| `--name "Name"` | the folder name | The project's display name. |
| `--slug <slug>` | the folder name, made lowercase with dashes | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Refused when another workspace on this Mac holds it. |
| `--owner "Name"`, `--email you@example.com` | `git config --global user.name` / `user.email` | The commit author written into `AGENTS.md`. With no identity, setup does not commit. |
| `--roles "qa security ..."` | all seven | `chief-of-staff` is always added. |
| `--runner <tool>` | the first installed of `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `qwen`, `grok`, `opencode`, `cursor`, else `claude` | The agent tool for scheduled jobs. `cursor` means the Cursor CLI, never the editor's `cursor` command. `custom` needs `--runner-cmd`. |
| `--runner-cmd '<command>'` | none | With `--runner custom`: the command to run, using `"$CABINET_PROMPT"` (and `$CABINET_AGENT`). No single quotes. |
| `--brief <when>` | `7:00 AM` | When the brief is written: a time every day (`"7 AM"`), or days and a time, one day (`"fri 4 PM"`) or several (`"sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"`), or `off`. See [Schedule times](#schedule-times). |
| `--week-start <day>` | `sunday` | Written into `AGENTS.md` house rules. |
| `--backup-dir <folder>` | `off` | Made absolute. Refused when it is inside the workspace or any repo it lists. |
| `--repo <git url>` | none | Repeatable. `https://`, `http://`, `ssh://`, `git://`, `file://`, `git@host:path`, an absolute path, or `./` / `../` (relative to the workspace). Two repos with the same name are refused. |
| `--dry-run` | | Prints everything setup would write and change, then stops: `Nothing was written.` |
| `--yes`, `-y` | | No questions: defaults and options only. |

Values written into `cabinet.env` (name, owner, email, backup folder) cannot contain `$`, a backtick, a backslash, a double quote or a line break.

**What it writes:** the project files from the kit's templates (`AGENTS.md`, `cabinet.env`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md`, `repos.tsv`, `jobs/brief.job`, `roles/`, `guides/`, `specs/`, `notes/`, `package.json`, `.gitignore`), the kit files (`CABINET.md`, `bin/`, `.cabinet/`), the built roles (`agents/`, `.claude/agents/`), and `CLAUDE.md` as a link to `AGENTS.md`. Then `git init` and one commit of those files. It records the slug in `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/workspace`.

**In a terminal, afterwards:** it offers `npm install` (to download the pinned kit) and `bin/bootstrap.sh` (shown as a dry run first, and applied only when you say yes).

**If it fails part way:** it removes the folder it created, or empties the empty folder it was given, and nothing else.

## cabinet init

```sh
cabinet init [dir] [options]
```

Adds cabinet to an existing folder (default: the current one). It takes every option of `cabinet new`, and these:

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `--inside` | In a project repo: the workspace is `cabinet/` inside it (the default there). |
| `--private` | With `--inside` (the default): `cabinet/` has its own git; the project's git ignores it and no tracked project file changes. |
| `--shared` | With `--inside`: `cabinet/` is part of the project's repo. Nothing is committed in the project; you review and commit. |
| `--beside` | In a project repo: the workspace is a folder next to it (default `<project>-hq`). |
| `--workspace <folder>` | With `--beside`: where that folder goes. |

What it does depends on where it runs (see [layouts](layouts.md)):

| Run in | Result |
|---|---|
| The top folder of a project repo | Inside (private or shared) or beside, asked or from the options. |
| A subfolder of a repo | Refused: run it at the repo's top folder. |
| A folder that is not a repo | The folder becomes the workspace, "around" what is there. The repos it finds in subfolders are listed in `repos.tsv`. |
| A folder that already has a workspace | Refused: use `cabinet update`. |

In every case, existing files are kept and reported, never replaced. Around a folder, a file of its own at a path the kit uses (such as `bin/doctor.sh`) stops setup before anything is written.

**What it reads from a project** (as defaults you can change):

- From `package.json`: the name (scope dropped: `@acme/shop` becomes `shop`), the description (quoted as the project's own words), the repository URL (when the repo has no `origin`), and the `test`, `dev`, `start`, `build`, `lint` and `typecheck` scripts (run with bun, pnpm or yarn when their lockfile is there). A value with shell characters, or a URL that is not a plain git URL, is not used.
- The project's own `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md`, named as where its rules live.
- The repo's own git `user.name` and `user.email` as the owner.

## cabinet next

```sh
cabinet next [--json]
```

Says what to do next in the workspace you are in, as a numbered list, and changes nothing: the `TBD` headings left in `AGENTS.md`, a workspace with no commits, a pinned kit not yet downloaded, a Mac without the push gate or schedules (`cabinet bootstrap`), handoffs waiting on the owner, today's brief (with when it was written) or when the first one comes, and how many problems the doctor finds. Outside a workspace it says how to start one. When nothing waits: `Nothing waits on you.` Each step ends with the command that does it, when there is one.

## cabinet list

```sh
cabinet list [--json]
```

Every workspace on this Mac, from anywhere: its slug, project name, kit version (marked `*` when it is not the installed kit), how many handoffs wait on you, what the doctor finds, when the latest brief was written, and its folder. The doctors run side by side, each with its workspace's own scripts, so it takes about as long as one doctor run. A workspace is listed once setup or bootstrap has claimed its slug on this Mac; `cabinet remove` takes it off the list. A workspace whose folder is gone shows as `folder gone`, with how to free its slug. Changes nothing. Exit 0.

## cabinet digest

```sh
cabinet digest [--json]
cabinet digest --write <file> [--notify]
cabinet digest --schedule [<when>|off] [--file <file>] [--notify]
```

One morning read for every workspace on this Mac: from each one's latest `BRIEF.md`, the "Sign-off queue" and "Actions for the owner" parts, by their `## ` headings (the chief-of-staff role writes them with these names), and how many handoffs wait on you. It flags a brief older than a day and a half (is the brief job running?), a workspace with no brief yet, and a brief without the "## Sign-off queue" heading. It reads only: you still answer each queue in its own workspace, to that workspace's agent. It starts with one line of counts (decisions, actions and handoffs waiting, and briefs late, missing or unreadable), and ends by saying whether it is scheduled.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `--write <file>` | Write the digest to that file (replaced each time) instead of the screen. |
| `--notify` | Also show a macOS notification with the counts line. |
| `--schedule [<when>]` | Write it on a schedule. With no time: every day at 10:00 AM. Or any [schedule time](#schedule-times): `"8 AM"`, `"fri 10 AM"`, `"sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"`. Run again to change it. `--schedule off` stops it and keeps the last file. |
| `--file <file>` | With `--schedule`: where it is written. Default `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/digest.md`, which a scheduled job can always write. macOS may block a scheduled job from writing to Documents, Desktop, Downloads or iCloud Drive until you allow it (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders); cabinet says so when you choose one. |
| `--json` | The digest as JSON (below). |

The schedule is one launchd job for the whole Mac, `ai.cabinet-digest`, apart from every workspace's `ai.cabinet.<slug>.*` jobs; it runs this `cabinet` (so install it globally, not only through npx, whose cache can be cleared) and logs to `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/digest.log`. The first notification may need you to allow notifications for Script Editor, which macOS uses to show them. Exit 0, or 1 for a bad time or a schedule launchd would not load.

## cabinet config

```sh
cabinet config [dir] [options]
```

Changes a workspace's settings after setup. Run it in the workspace, or in the project's top folder when the workspace is `cabinet/` inside it. In a terminal it asks the setup questions again with the current answers as defaults, lists the changes, and asks before writing.

Options: `--name`, `--slug`, `--owner`, `--email`, `--roles`, `--runner`, `--runner-cmd`, `--brief`, `--week-start`, `--backup-dir`, `--backup-time <time>` (like `"1 PM"`), `--repo` (adds a repo; to remove one, edit `repos.tsv`), `--apply` (run `bin/bootstrap.sh` without asking), `--dry-run` (list the changes and write nothing), `--yes`.

**For this Mac only:** `cabinet config --this-mac --backup-dir <folder>|off [--backup-time <time>]` writes the backup settings into `cabinet.local.env` instead of `cabinet.env`, so they apply on this Mac and are never committed. In a shared workspace, each teammate picks their own backup folder, or none. `cabinet config --this-mac --clear` makes this Mac follow `cabinet.env` again. With `--this-mac`, no other setting can be changed (they are shared by every Mac), and nothing is asked.

**What it changes:**

| Setting | Where |
|---|---|
| Name | `CABINET_PROJECT`, and the titles setup wrote in `AGENTS.md`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md`, `specs/ROADMAP.md`, plus the workspace's own `package.json` |
| Slug | `CABINET_SLUG`; stops the old schedules, renames them in `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md` and `jobs/*.job`, claims the new slug and releases the old one, and says how to move the backup passphrase in the keychain |
| Owner and email | the "Commits" line in `AGENTS.md` |
| Roles | `CABINET_ROLES`, the team tables in `AGENTS.md` and `OPERATIONS.md` (a dropped role's row leaves; a returning kit role's row comes back; a project role gets a `TBD` row), and the built roles |
| Runner | `CABINET_RUNNER`, `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD` |
| Brief | `WHEN` in `jobs/brief.job` |
| Week start | the house rule in `AGENTS.md` |
| Backups | `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` |
| Repos | new rows in `repos.tsv` and the team table in `AGENTS.md` |

Roles the project defines itself (`roles/<role>.md` with frontmatter) are accepted and asked about. Layout and visibility (inside, beside, private, shared) are not changed by `config`. When nothing changes, it prints `Nothing to change.` and writes nothing.

## cabinet remove

```sh
cabinet remove [dir] [--dry-run] [--yes] [--force] [--delete-key]
```

Removes a workspace from this Mac. It first prints the plan:

- stop and delete the workspace's own schedules (a plist is its own when it runs this workspace's `bin/`; another workspace's are never touched);
- delete its log folder `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/`, which frees the slug;
- the backup passphrase and archives stay, unless `--delete-key` (archives always stay);
- inside a project, private: remove the pointers in `CLAUDE.local.md`, `QWEN.local.md` and an untracked `AGENTS.md` (a file left empty is deleted), the role files setup built in `.claude/agents/`, and their `.git/info/exclude` lines, so the project is as it was before `init`;
- inside a project, shared: remove the "Agent team" section from `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` and the `@tarekraafat/cabinet` devDependency; you commit that change;
- delete the workspace folder.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `[dir]` | Default: the workspace you are in. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the plan only. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | Do not ask. Without it you type the slug to confirm. |
| `--force` | Go ahead even when the workspace has uncommitted changes or commits on no remote. Without it, those stop the removal (`Not safe to delete`). |
| `--delete-key` | Also delete the keychain item `cabinet.<slug>.backup`. |

The guardrails in your agent tools stay, since other workspaces use them. Exit codes: 0, or 1 when refused or not confirmed.

## cabinet update

```sh
cabinet update [dir]
```

Copies the installed kit's files into the workspace, rebuilds the roles, and prints every changelog section between the workspace's old version and the new one. It never replaces a kit file that was edited in the workspace: it stops, names the file, and keeps the old version (exit 1). It ends with the exact `git add` and `git commit` to run.

## cabinet status

```sh
cabinet status [dir] [--json]
```

Prints the workspace's kit version, the installed kit's version, and every kit file edited in the workspace. `--json` prints `{workspace, version, kit_version, kit, edited}`.

## cabinet outdated

```sh
cabinet outdated [dir]
```

Compares the workspace's kit version, the installed kit and the newest version on the npm registry, and says what to run. Without the registry it says the newest is unknown. Exit 0.

## cabinet changelog

```sh
cabinet changelog [from-version]
```

Prints the changelog sections newer than `from-version` (all of them when it is left out).

## cabinet completion

```sh
eval "$(cabinet completion zsh)"     # in ~/.zshrc
eval "$(cabinet completion bash)"    # in ~/.bashrc
```

Tab completion for commands, their options, and the job names of the nearest workspace after `cabinet run`.

## cabinet version

Prints the installed kit's version.

## Which copy of cabinet runs

`cabinet update`, `status` and `config` hand off to the workspace's own pinned copy when it exists (`<workspace>/node_modules/@tarekraafat/cabinet`, or the project's `node_modules` above a shared `cabinet/`), so they always act with the project's version. They do this only in a cabinet workspace: the folder named, or the nearest workspace from the current folder upward. `new`, `init`, `changelog` and `version` always run the copy you called.

## Workspace scripts

All of them read `cabinet.env`. Run each as its `cabinet` command from anywhere in the workspace or its project, or as the script itself (`cabinet/bin/<script>` inside a project).

| Command | Script |
|---|---|
| `cabinet doctor` | `bin/doctor.sh` |
| `cabinet bootstrap` | `bin/bootstrap.sh` |
| `cabinet brief` | `bin/scheduled.sh brief` |
| `cabinet run <job>` | `bin/scheduled.sh <job>` |
| `cabinet handoffs` | `bin/handoffs.sh` |
| `cabinet handoff` | `bin/handoff.sh` |
| `cabinet archive` | `bin/archive-handoffs.sh` |
| `cabinet secrets` | `bin/secrets.sh` |
| `cabinet roles` | `bin/roles.sh` |
| `cabinet backup` | `bin/backup.sh` |
| `cabinet restore` | `bin/restore.sh` (outside any workspace, the installed kit's copy: a new Mac has no workspace yet) |
| `cabinet snapshot` | `bin/snapshot.sh` |
| `cabinet move` | `bin/move.sh` |

| Script | What it does | Exit codes |
|---|---|---|
| `bin/bootstrap.sh [--dry-run] [--no-schedules \| --schedules]` | Sets up this Mac for the workspace: clones missing repos, restores local-only files, links `CLAUDE.md`, gives each repo whose owner is `TBD` a builder ([concepts](concepts.md#the-team)), builds the roles, installs the guardrails ([guardrails](guardrails.md)) and the workspace's secrets check before each commit, and adds, updates or removes the schedules to match `jobs/` and the backup setting. `--dry-run` only prints. `--no-schedules` stops and from then on skips the jobs' schedules on this Mac, for a workspace whose jobs another Mac runs (a teammate's, in a shared workspace); `--schedules` undoes it. Both are saved in `cabinet.local.env`. The backup schedule is not affected. Safe to rerun. | 0, or 1 when any step did not complete (each one says why) |
| `bin/doctor.sh [--fix [--yes]] [--json]` | Checks everything: repos, kit files, roles, guardrails for every installed tool, the manual, handoff IDs, secrets in the workspace's files, uncommitted work, schedules, backups. It starts with a summary (`N thing(s) need attention:` and the list, or `All good.`), then the full report. Changes nothing in the workspace or your settings (it runs `opencode debug` and `grok inspect`, which may write their own caches). `--fix` then runs the fixes it knows (`bin/bootstrap.sh`, `bin/roles.sh`, `bin/snapshot.sh`), asking before each unless `--yes`, and checks again. `--json` prints the results for scripts (see [Output for agents and scripts](#output-for-agents-and-scripts)). Every message is explained in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). | 0, or 1 when anything says FIX |
| `bin/handoffs.sh [name] [--json]` | Without a name: every open handoff with its age in days, oldest first (`?` when it has no date). With a repo or role name (`qa`, `owner`): every entry addressed to it, in full. | 0 |
| `bin/handoff.sh --from <name> --to <name> --changed "..." --needed "..." [--depends-on "..."] "<title>"` | Files one handoff: appends the entry at the bottom of "Open" in `HANDOFFS.md` with the next free ID for today (`H-20261019-01`, unique across `HANDOFFS.md` and the archives), today's date, status `open` and the template's lines, then commits it on its own (`handoffs: <ID> <title>`). `--depends-on` defaults to `none`. Each value is kept on one line. It prints the new ID first. When `HANDOFFS.md` already has someone else's uncommitted lines, it writes the entry but does not commit, so their lines never go into its commit. Two agents filing at once get different IDs. | 0, 1 when the commit failed (the entry is written) or `HANDOFFS.md` has no "## Open" heading, 2 for a missing value or unknown option |
| `bin/archive-handoffs.sh` | Moves every committed `done` or `rejected` handoff to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` and commits the move. | 0, or 1 when `HANDOFFS.md` has uncommitted lines |
| `bin/secrets.sh [--staged]` | Looks for keys, tokens and passwords in the workspace's own files (tracked, and new files git does not ignore; not the product repos, which have their own git): private key blocks; AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe live, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google API and npm keys; and lines that set a password, secret, token or API key to a value that is not a placeholder (`<...>`) or a variable (`$X`). It prints each file and line with the kind of secret, never the value. A false alarm: add `not-a-secret` anywhere on its line. `--staged` checks only the lines staged for the next commit; the workspace's pre-commit hook runs it ([guardrails](guardrails.md#what-bootstrap-installs)). | 0, or 1 when something is found (with `--staged`, the commit is refused) |
| `bin/roles.sh [--check]` | Builds `agents/<role>.md` and `.claude/agents/<role>.md` (and, inside a project, the project's `.claude/agents/` and pointer files). `--check` only reports. | 0, or 1 when a role is missing or out of date |
| `bin/scheduled.sh <job>` | Runs `jobs/<job>.job` now with the configured runner, logging to `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/<job>.log`. | 0, 1 when the run failed, 2 for an unknown or incomplete job |
| `bin/backup.sh [--verify] [folder]` | One encrypted backup now ([backups](backups.md)). Default folder: `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`. `--verify` writes nothing there: it restores the newest archive into a temporary folder, checks each repo against the workspace, and deletes the copy ([backups](backups.md#checking-it)). | 0, 1 with no passphrase (or, with `--verify`, no archive or a problem found), 2 for a missing, relative or inside folder, or a keep count under 1 |
| `bin/restore.sh <archive> [folder]` | Rebuilds the workspace and its repos from an archive, never losing a file ([backups](backups.md)). It starts by naming the backup's date. | 0, or 1 with no passphrase |
| `bin/snapshot.sh` | Copies each repo's local-only files and `.git/info/exclude` entries into `local/<repo>/`. The backup runs it first. | 0 |
| `bin/move.sh <new-path> [--dry-run]` | Moves a workspace folder and updates what remembers its path: Claude Code's memory and trusted folders, Codex's trusted folders, the schedules. Refused for the inside and beside layouts. | 0, or 1 when refused |

## Output for agents and scripts

Text output is for people and may be reworded at any time. For a script or an agent, use JSON: a field or ID is never renamed or removed without a changelog entry that says so.

| Command | Prints |
|---|---|
| `cabinet help --json`, `cabinet help <command> --json` | `{name, version, docs, commands: [{name, group, usage, summary, options: [{name, value, text}]}]}` |
| `cabinet next --json` | `{workspace, project, steps: [{id, text, command}], optional: [...]}`. Step IDs: `tbd`, `commit`, `install`, `bootstrap`, `handoffs`, `brief`, `doctor`; `command` is empty when the step is not a command. Outside a workspace, `workspace` is `null` and the one step is `start`. |
| `cabinet doctor --json` | `{workspace, problems, notes, can_fix, results: [{level, section, id, message}]}`. `level` is `ok`, `fix` or `note`; `id` names the check (every ID is in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)) and does not change when its message is reworded. Exit 1 when `problems` is above 0. |
| `cabinet handoffs --json` | The open and acknowledged entries, oldest first: `[{id, status, status_line, date, age_days, from, to, title}]`. `date` and `age_days` are `null` when the status line has no date. |
| `cabinet handoffs <name> --json` | Every entry addressed to that repo or role and not closed, with its full `text`. `owner` and `founder` are the same person. |
| `cabinet status --json` | `{workspace, version, kit_version, kit, edited}` |
| `cabinet digest --json` | `[{slug, project, path, exists, brief_written, brief_stale, sign_off_queue, queue_heading_found, actions_for_owner, waiting_on_owner}]`. The two parts are the Markdown under their headings, or `null`; `queue_heading_found` is `null` with no brief. |
| `cabinet list --json` | `[{slug, project, path, exists, version, update_available, waiting_on_owner, doctor_problems, brief_written}]`. `brief_written` is ISO 8601 UTC, or `null`; the counts are `null` for a workspace whose folder is gone. |

## Files you can edit

### cabinet.env

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CABINET_PROJECT` | Display name. |
| `CABINET_SLUG` | Short name for everything machine-wide. Change it with `cabinet config --slug`. |
| `CABINET_ROLES` | Roles to build, space separated. |
| `CABINET_RUNNER` | `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `qwen`, `grok`, `opencode`, `cursor` or `custom`. |
| `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD` | With `custom`: the command, single-quoted. |
| `CABINET_LAYOUT` | `new`, `around`, `inside` or `beside`. Set by setup; not changed by `config`. |
| `CABINET_VISIBILITY` | Inside only: `private` or `shared`. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR` | Absolute folder for archives, outside the workspace and its repos; empty turns backups off. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` | Time of the daily backup, like `1:00 PM` (default). |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_KEEP` | How many of this workspace's archives to keep (default 14, at least 1). |
| `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT` | Minutes a job may run before it is stopped, for jobs without their own `TIMEOUT` (default 60; `0` for no limit). |
| `CABINET_SKILLS`, `CABINET_PLUGINS` | Claude Code skills and plugins the doctor expects (a missing one is a note). |

### jobs/&lt;job&gt;.job

One scheduled agent run each. Keys: `AGENT` (the role), `PROMPT`, `WHEN` (a [schedule time](#schedule-times), or empty for by hand only), `MINUTES` and `RESULT` (shown when run by hand), `TIMEOUT` (whole minutes before the run is stopped, with everything it started, and the reason written to its log; empty uses `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT`, `0` means no limit), `AFTER` (an optional shell command run in the workspace after a successful run). After a change, run `bin/bootstrap.sh`.

### cabinet.local.env

Settings for this Mac only. Git never tracks it (the workspace's `.gitignore` tracks only its own files), so in a shared workspace each teammate's Mac keeps its own. It is read, never run as shell. Its keys:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CABINET_SCHEDULES` | `off`: this Mac schedules none of the jobs in `jobs/` (another Mac runs them). Set and cleared with `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules` and `--schedules`. Jobs still run by hand with `cabinet run <job>`. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` | When present, they replace `cabinet.env`'s on this Mac; an empty `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR` turns backups off here. Set with `cabinet config --this-mac`, removed with `cabinet config --this-mac --clear`. |

### Schedule times

Every schedule takes the same forms: the brief (`--brief`), any job (`WHEN` in `jobs/<job>.job`) and the digest (`cabinet digest --schedule`).

| Form | Means |
|---|---|
| `7 AM`, `7:00 AM`, `7am`, `daily 7 AM` | Every day at 7:00 AM. |
| `fri 4 PM`, `Friday 4:00 PM` | Every Friday at 4:00 PM. |
| `fri,sat 10:30 AM` | Every Friday and Saturday at 10:30 AM. |
| `sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM` | Sunday to Thursday at 8:00 AM. |
| `12 PM`, `12 AM` | Noon, midnight. |

Times are 12-hour, with `AM` or `PM` in any case (`pm`, `p.m.` too); the minutes can be left out (`4 PM`). A time without AM or PM is read as 24-hour (`16:00` is 4:00 PM, `7:00` is 7:00 AM), so files and scripts written that way keep working; a bare hour (`10`) is refused, since it could be either. Put a time with a space in quotes on the command line: `--brief "fri 4 PM"`.

Days are `sun`, `mon`, `tue`, `wed`, `thu`, `fri`, `sat`, or their full names, in any case, separated by commas. All the days named share one time. Naming all seven is the same as every day. Setup and config store one form, `fri,sat 10:30 AM`, and every message shows times as `4:00 PM`.

### repos.tsv

Tab separated, one row per repo: name, clone URL (`-` for none), local-only files (space separated, `-` for none), `CLAUDE.md` link (`yes` or `no`), and an optional path where the repo lives (absolute, `~/...`, or relative to the workspace; default `<workspace>/<name>`). Windows line endings are fine. A row whose name is not a plain folder name is skipped with a message.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` | backup, restore | The archive passphrase, instead of the keychain item `cabinet.<slug>.backup`. Never put it in `cabinet.env`, which git tracks. |
| `CABINET_PROMPT`, `CABINET_AGENT` | the `custom` runner | The prompt and role, for `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD`. |
| `CABINET_TTY` | setup, config, remove | Read answers from this file instead of the terminal (the tests use it). |
| `CABINET_PRIVATE_WORDS` | `npm test` | Words that must not appear in the kit. |

## Removing a workspace

`cabinet remove` does all of this (see [cabinet remove](#cabinet-remove)). By hand:

1. Stop its schedules: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>` for each, then delete `~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.cabinet.<slug>.*.plist`.
2. Delete its log folder `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/`, which also frees the slug.
3. If it had backups: `security delete-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup`, and delete its archives if you no longer want them.
4. Delete the workspace folder.
5. Inside a project: for private, remove the `/cabinet/`, `/CLAUDE.local.md`, `/QWEN.local.md`, `/AGENTS.md` (if setup created it) and `/.claude/agents/<role>.md` lines from the project's `.git/info/exclude`, and the files they name if setup made them; for shared, remove the "Agent team" section and the `@tarekraafat/cabinet` devDependency from the project.

The guardrails stay; see [guardrails](guardrails.md#undoing-the-guardrails).


========================================================================
File: docs/layouts.md
========================================================================

# Layouts

Where a workspace sits, and what that means for your project. `cabinet new` makes the first; `cabinet init` picks one of the other three from where you run it. The layout is recorded as `CABINET_LAYOUT` in `cabinet.env` and does not change later.

| Layout | Made by | The workspace is | Your project |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new` | `cabinet new <dir>` | a new folder; product repos are cloned into it | (cloned into the workspace) |
| `around` | `cabinet init` in a folder that is not a repo | that folder, around what is already in it | the repos in its subfolders, listed in `repos.tsv` |
| `inside` | `cabinet init --inside` in a project repo | `cabinet/` inside the project | unchanged files, plus what is listed below |
| `beside` | `cabinet init --beside` in a project repo | a folder next to the project (default `<project>-hq`) | not changed at all |

## new

The simplest: one folder holding the team's files and, under it, every product repo (cloned by `bin/bootstrap.sh` from `repos.tsv`). The workspace's `.gitignore` tracks only its own files, so the product repos stay out of its git.

## around

For a folder that already holds your repos side by side. `cabinet init` keeps everything there: existing files are never replaced, the folder's own `.gitignore` is kept, and only the files setup placed are committed (never a `.env` or other files that were already there). The repos it finds are listed in `repos.tsv`. If the folder already has a file at a path the kit uses, such as `bin/doctor.sh`, setup stops before writing anything: rename or move that file, then run `cabinet init` again.

## inside

For one project repo that should carry its team with it. The workspace is `<project>/cabinet/`. Agents usually start in the project's top folder, so setup points them at `cabinet/` with an "Agent team" section, and also writes the role definitions into the project's `.claude/agents/` (a file of the project's own with the same name is kept). Paths in `CABINET.md` and the roles are relative to `cabinet/`: run its scripts as `cabinet/bin/<script>`. `cabinet status`, `update` and `config` work from the project's top folder.

There are two kinds, set once as `CABINET_VISIBILITY`:

### Private (the default)

`cabinet/` has its own git, and the project's git never sees it. No tracked file of the project changes:

- the pointer goes only into files the project does not track: `CLAUDE.local.md` (read by Claude Code and Grok), `QWEN.local.md` (Qwen), and `AGENTS.md` only when the project has none;
- `cabinet/`, those pointer files and the role files are added to the project's `.git/info/exclude`;
- the version pin goes in `cabinet/package.json`;
- `bin/roles.sh` rebuilds the pointers on every update and after a restore.

When the project has its own `AGENTS.md`, it is left alone. Codex, opencode, Gemini and Cursor read only that file, so start them in `cabinet/`, or add the "Agent team" section to `AGENTS.md` yourself. If you later write a real `AGENTS.md` for a project that had none, remove `/AGENTS.md` from `.git/info/exclude` first, or git will ignore it.

Fits: solo work, open source projects, client repos.

### Shared

`cabinet/` is part of the project's repo, for everyone who clones it. Setup adds the "Agent team" section to the project's `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`, or a new `AGENTS.md`) and pins the kit in the project's `package.json` as a devDependency (with npm's own `npm pkg set`: formatting kept, no network, an existing entry left alone). Setup commits nothing in the project: review the new files and commit them yourself. Without a `package.json` in the project, the pin goes in `cabinet/package.json`.

Fits: a private repo whose teammates should see the team's handoffs and specs.

## beside

The project is not changed at all. The workspace is a folder next to it and points at it with a relative path (`../<project>`) in `repos.tsv`, so the project stays where it is and nothing is cloned again. Fits a product with several repos, or a project you would rather not touch.

## What lives where

| | What | Who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| **Kit files** | `CABINET.md`, `bin/*.sh`, `.cabinet/` (roles, guardrails, schedule template, version, manifest) | Only `cabinet update`. Never edit them in a workspace: an update stops at an edited one. |
| **Project files** | `AGENTS.md`, `cabinet.env`, `roles/`, `jobs/`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `repos.tsv`, `specs/`, `notes/` | You and the agents. Placed once by `new` or `init`; afterwards `cabinet config` changes only the settings it manages in them. |
| **Built** | `agents/<role>.md`, `.claude/agents/<role>.md`: the kit's role plus your `roles/<role>.md` | `bin/roles.sh` |

Instructions layer from general to specific: `CABINET.md`, then the workspace's `AGENTS.md`, then each repo's own `AGENTS.md`.

## Switching layouts

Not supported: moving between layouts, or between private and shared, means moving files and changing git by hand. `bin/move.sh` moves a `new` or `around` workspace to another folder; it refuses the inside and beside layouts, whose relative paths would break.


========================================================================
File: docs/concepts.md
========================================================================

# Concepts

The ideas cabinet is built on. The rules themselves are in `CABINET.md`, which every workspace gets and every agent reads first; this page explains them for people.

## The team

A workspace runs a product with AI agents, each in a role, and one owner (you) who signs off. The kit's roles:

| Role | Owns | Decides | Brings to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| chief-of-staff | the brief, the sign-off queue, routing tasks, seats | how work is routed | every decision in one queue |
| product-manager | one spec per feature, the roadmap | nothing you have not decided | product decisions, framed with a recommendation |
| architect | contracts between repos, architecture decision records | reversible technical questions across repos | vendors, data handling, public API shapes |
| qa | independent verification | PASS or BLOCK | overrides of a block |
| security | security and privacy review of unpushed work | PASS or BLOCK | legal and disclosure questions |
| design-lead | UX and visual consistency inside the brand guide | layout and interaction choices | any brand change |
| finance | cost and pricing models | how to model | every price, plan and spend |
| backend, web, mobile, infrastructure | the product repos the team table assigns each (the builders) | how to build inside a repo, following its own conventions | changes to a repo's stack or tools; applying infrastructure |

Each role's file says what it owns, decides, escalates and may write. A project turns roles on or off (`CABINET_ROLES`), adds notes to one in `roles/<role>.md`, or defines its own role there.

**Builders** are the roles that write the product's code. They are not in `CABINET_ROLES`: a builder is built when it owns a repo in the team table of `AGENTS.md`. When a repo whose owner is `TBD` first arrives on a Mac, `bin/bootstrap.sh` gives it the builder it most looks like: `mobile` for an `ios/` or `android/` folder, a `pubspec.yaml`, an Xcode project, or React Native or Expo; `infrastructure` for Terraform, Pulumi, Helm or CDK files; `web` for React, Next, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Astro or Nuxt, or an `index.html`; otherwise `backend`. Change the row to choose another builder, a project role, or `owner`, then `bin/roles.sh`. In a repo that already exists a builder learns how it is built (its `AGENTS.md`, scripts, CI, lint and style) and follows it; only a new, empty repo gets defaults (`CABINET.md`, "Builders").

## Rules, guides and notes

What the agents follow, from the most general to the most specific:

1. `CABINET.md`: how every cabinet workspace runs. From the kit; never edited in a workspace.
2. `AGENTS.md` in the workspace: this project's team, contracts, house rules and product rules, and the "Guides" table.
3. `guides/`: standing documents, such as a brand guide, style guide, policy or business document. Agents read a guide before any work its row in `AGENTS.md` covers. A guide ranks with `AGENTS.md`.
4. `roles/<role>.md`: what this project adds for one role, built into that role's definition.
5. A repo's own `AGENTS.md`: rules for work in that repo.

On a conflict the more specific wins: a repo's `AGENTS.md` over the workspace's `AGENTS.md` and guides, over `CABINET.md`. Nothing can loosen "Never push, merge, publish or release" or "The builder never verifies". `notes/` is different: thinking and decisions on the record, read when relevant, not rules in force. How to add each: [recipes](recipes.md#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents).

## Repo ownership

Each repo has one owning agent, listed in the team table in `AGENTS.md`. No agent writes to a repo it does not own. When a change affects another repo, the agent files a handoff instead of editing it.

## Handoffs

`HANDOFFS.md` is the one channel between agents. Each entry has an ID (`H-20261018-01`), who it is from and to, a status (`open`, `acknowledged`, `done`, `rejected`), what changed, what is needed, and what it depends on. The addressee edits only the status line; everyone else adds a follow-up entry. Closed entries move to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` daily. `bin/handoff.sh` files an entry with the next free ID and commits it; `bin/handoffs.sh <name>` shows an agent its open entries.

## Decision tiers

Every decision belongs to exactly one tier:

1. **The agent:** reversible and inside its own files, following existing rules.
2. **The function's lead:** reversible, crosses repos or sets direction, costs nothing.
3. **You:** irreversible, public, or costs money. Pushes, deploys, publishing, prices, spend, brand, legal, and adding or changing an agent.

An agent unsure of the tier treats it as the higher one. A reversible tier 3 item marked "default" may go ahead as local commits after 72 hours without an objection, but nothing is ever pushed, published or spent on silence.

## The brief and the sign-off queue

The chief-of-staff writes `BRIEF.md` on a schedule (`jobs/brief.job`). It verifies handoffs against git, checks the repos and the doctor, and puts every decision waiting on you at the top. Each decision has a plain question, lettered options with their consequences, each expert's recommendation, one overall recommendation, and whether it can be undone. You answer in one message; the agents apply your answers. Its parts sit under fixed headings (`## Sign-off queue`, `## Actions for the owner`, ...), so with several projects `cabinet digest` gathers every queue into one read.

## The builder never verifies

Work is ready for you to push only when qa and security have each recorded PASS on its handoff (and design-lead for UI work). A BLOCK holds the push until it is fixed or you override it.

## Seats

A seat is a role filled by an agent or a person. The chief-of-staff flags signs that a seat is needed (recurring work no seat owns, a function falling behind) with evidence only, and every new seat is your decision, with its cost and the alternatives. Each new seat goes through an onboarding checklist and a review after a month.

## Slugs and isolation

Every workspace has a slug. Everything it puts on the Mac is named by it: schedules `ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>`, logs `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/`, the backup key `cabinet.<slug>.backup`, archives `<slug>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.tar.gz.enc`. The log folder holds a `workspace` file naming its owner. Setup and `cabinet config` refuse a slug another workspace holds, bootstrap never replaces or removes a schedule that runs another workspace, and backup cleanup removes only the slug's own archives. Paths are compared with symlinks resolved, so a workspace reached through a link is still the same one.

## Agent tools and models

cabinet works through agent tools, so it works with any model they offer. Everything is plain files: any tool that reads `AGENTS.md` can run the team, and acting as a role means reading `agents/<role>.md`. Scheduled jobs run with the tool in `CABINET_RUNNER`. Which tools have guardrails, and their limits: [guardrails](guardrails.md).

| Runner | Runs a job as |
|---|---|
| `claude` | `claude -p --agent <role> --permission-mode auto` (tested with real scheduled jobs) |
| `codex` | `codex exec "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `gemini` | `gemini -p "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `qwen` | `qwen --approval-mode auto "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `grok` | `grok -p "<role instruction> <prompt>" --permission-mode auto` |
| `opencode` | `opencode run "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `cursor` | `cursor-agent -p --force "<role instruction> <prompt>"` (run live) |
| `custom` | `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD`, with the prompt in `$CABINET_PROMPT` and the role in `$CABINET_AGENT` |

The role instruction is "Act as the <role> role: read agents/<role>.md and follow it as your instructions". Runners other than `claude` and `cursor` follow each tool's documented headless mode and are untested end to end; Codex's default sandbox and Gemini's default approvals may not let a scheduled brief write its file. Scheduled jobs get a PATH with the runner's and Node's folders.


========================================================================
File: docs/guardrails.md
========================================================================

# Guardrails

How cabinet keeps every push, merge, release and publish with you, what each agent tool's rules can and cannot block, and how to undo them.

## The two layers

1. **The push gate.** A global git pre-push hook asks for `yes` at your terminal for every `git push`, from any tool. Agents run without a terminal, so their pushes are refused.
2. **Deny rules in each agent tool.** They block push, merge, release and publish commands, and the known ways around the push gate (git can be told to skip hooks).

Together they are a strong speed bump, not a boundary. For a hard boundary, protect your branches on the server (GitHub branch protection).

## What bootstrap installs

`bin/bootstrap.sh` installs the guardrails machine-wide, for every tool it finds. It is safe with several workspaces: rules are only ever added, never removed; a config file that is not plain JSON, or whose shape is unexpected, is left exactly as it was, with a message; files are written in place, so their permissions and symlinks stay; and a backup copy `<file>.bak.<timestamp>` is made before any change. A file that already exists (the push gate, the Codex rules, the Gemini policy) is left as it is and checked, never replaced.

| Tool | Reads `AGENTS.md` | Guardrails | Checked by `bin/doctor.sh` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | through the `CLAUDE.md` link | `~/.claude/settings.json` `permissions.deny` / `ask` | yes |
| Grok | yes, in folders you trust | reads the Claude Code rules | yes, with `grok inspect` |
| Qwen Code | yes | `~/.qwen/settings.json`, the same rule list | yes |
| opencode | yes | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` `permission.bash`, placed last because its last matching rule wins. A commented `opencode.jsonc` is never rewritten; opencode reads it after the `.json`, so a rule there can still override | on opencode 1.x; on 2.x it cannot (its debug commands need a background service), so check by hand |
| Gemini CLI | bootstrap sets `context.fileName` in `~/.gemini/settings.json` | `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml` | yes |
| Codex | yes | `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`; also `approval_policy = "on-request"` in `~/.codex/config.toml`, so Codex asks before anything its sandbox does not allow | yes |
| Antigravity CLI | yes | its `settings.json` | yes |
| Cursor CLI (`cursor-agent` / `agent`) | yes | `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` `permissions.deny` | yes (the file) |
| Cursor editor | yes | none: its agent's command rules live in the editor's own settings, which the kit does not change. The push gate applies | noted |
| Any other tool | point it at `AGENTS.md` | the push gate only | named, as a note |

Two more machine-wide settings come with the push gate:

- **`git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.config/git/hooks`**, where the gate lives. A global hooks path makes git skip every repo's own `.git/hooks`, so bootstrap also places a pass-through stub there for the other client hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, post-checkout and the rest; not push-to-checkout or fsmonitor-watchman, which change git's behavior just by existing). A repo's own hooks, such as a secret scanner, keep running. A repo that sets its own `core.hooksPath` (husky does) bypasses the gate; the doctor names it.
- **The workspace's secrets check,** a `pre-commit` hook in the workspace's own `.git/hooks` (bootstrap runs it through the pass-through stub). It runs `bin/secrets.sh --staged` and refuses a commit that adds a likely key, token or password, naming the file and line, never the value. A false alarm passes once its line has `not-a-secret` on it. An existing `pre-commit` hook is left as it is (the doctor notes it; your hook can call `bin/secrets.sh --staged` itself). A shared `cabinet/` inside a project gets none, since the project's own hooks run there; `bin/doctor.sh` still scans its files. It is a safety net, not a guarantee: it knows common key formats, not every secret.
- **Gemini CLI's `context.fileName`** is set to read `AGENTS.md` everywhere, so Gemini also loads `AGENTS.md` in folders that are not cabinet workspaces.

## What each tool's rules block

The rule formats differ, so the coverage does too.

**Claude Code, Grok, Qwen Code, opencode** (one rule list, matched anywhere in a command, so also inside wrappers such as `env`, `bash -c` or `nohup`):

- push, `git send-pack` (which pushes without hooks), merge, release, `gh api` writes, publishing (npm, npx, bun, pnpm, yarn, also with options before `publish`);
- the ways around the gate: `-c core.hooksPath` in common spellings, `GIT_CONFIG_*` variables, `env -i` and `env -u`, a push behind a `HOME=` override (caught because `git push` is matched anywhere), `--no-verify` and its abbreviations, faking a terminal (`script`, `expect`, `unbuffer`, Python's `pty.spawn`);
- printing the GitHub token, and reading the keychain.

Side effects: some harmless commands are refused too, such as an npm script named like `publish-docs`, or any command that mentions `git push` (for example in an `echo`).

**Gemini CLI** (regular expressions): the same list, with the hooks path matched in any letter case and `git push` matched anywhere in a command.

**Cursor CLI** (the command's first word plus an arguments pattern): push, `send-pack`, hook-path and `--no-verify` arguments to git, the terminal fakers, merges, releases, `gh api` writes, publishing, the GitHub token and the keychain. Probed live on Cursor CLI 2026.10.16 with harmless stand-ins:

- argument patterns match at the start and in the middle; first-word rules match;
- chained commands (`a && b`) are checked;
- a leading variable (`HOME=... git push`) is dropped before matching, so the git rules still catch it;
- wrappers are not looked through, so the kit denies `env`, `bash -c`, `sh -c`, `zsh -c`, `nohup`, `xargs`, `sudo`, `exec`, `command`, `nice` and `stdbuf` outright, and `timeout` or `time` with push, publish or `send-pack`. Any other wrapper is not caught.

**Codex and Antigravity** (rules match only how a command starts): push, `send-pack`, `env -i` and `env -u`, merge, release, publish and the terminal fakers are denied; `git -c ...` and `gh api` ask first. A bypass that does not start the command, such as `HOME=... git push` or `--no-verify` after other words, is not caught.

**Not caught by any tool's rules:** git config keys in unusual letter case (except in Gemini), an agent editing `.git/config` with its file tools (the doctor reports a repo's own `core.hooksPath` afterwards), and other ways of faking a terminal.

## Known limits

These are on the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md):

- archives are encrypted with AES-256-CBC and no separate integrity check, so tampering shows only as an unreadable archive;
- any process of your user can read the backup passphrase from the keychain without a prompt (the deny rules stop agents in the tools above);
- opencode agent-level and project-level configs, and Qwen workspace settings, can loosen the global rules, and the doctor checks only the global result;
- on opencode 2.x the doctor cannot read the resolved rules.

## Undoing the guardrails

The guardrails are shared by every workspace on the Mac, so removing a workspace leaves them. To remove them:

- **Rules in a tool's settings:** restore the `.bak.<timestamp>` copy bootstrap made next to the file, or delete the rules you no longer want (the kit's list is in each workspace's `.cabinet/guardrails/`).
- **The push gate and hook stubs:** `git config --global --unset core.hooksPath`, then delete `~/.config/git/hooks/`.
- **Codex:** remove `approval_policy` from `~/.codex/config.toml` and the kit's rules from `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`.
- **Gemini:** delete `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml` and remove `context.fileName` from `~/.gemini/settings.json`.


========================================================================
File: docs/backups.md
========================================================================

# Backups

An encrypted daily archive of everything a lost Mac would take with it, and a restore that never loses a file.

## What a backup holds

`bin/backup.sh` writes one archive with, for the workspace and every repo in `repos.tsv`:

- the full git history: every branch and unpushed commit;
- uncommitted changes, untracked files and stashes;
- `.env` files (git ignores them, so nothing else keeps them);
- the branch it was on, or that HEAD was detached.

It also includes Claude Code's memory for the workspace and `~/.claude/settings.json`. A repo with no commits yet (for example a workspace made without an owner identity) is kept as its files.

Archives are named `<slug>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.tar.gz.enc`, encrypted with AES-256-CBC (PBKDF2, 200000 iterations), readable only by you (mode 600). The newest `CABINET_BACKUP_KEEP` (default 14) of this workspace's archives are kept; another workspace's archives in the same folder are never touched.

## Setting it up

1. Choose a folder **outside** the workspace and every repo it lists: a synced drive or an external disk. Setup, `cabinet config` and the backup itself refuse a folder inside them, because a backup there is lost with what it protects, copies itself into every later archive, and can be committed.
2. Set it with `cabinet config --backup-dir <folder>` (and `--backup-time "<time>"`, default 1:00 PM), then `bin/bootstrap.sh` to schedule it.
3. Put the passphrase in the keychain, and keep the same one in your password manager: without it no archive opens.

```sh
security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup -w
```

Or set `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` in the environment. Never put it in `cabinet.env`, which git tracks.

## Restoring

```sh
bin/restore.sh <archive> [folder]     # folder: where the workspace goes (default: this workspace)
bin/bootstrap.sh                      # then guardrails, links and schedules
bin/doctor.sh
```

On a new Mac, put the passphrase in the keychain first, then run `restore.sh` from a copy of the kit (or a clone of the workspace's repo). Restore never loses a file:

- **A repo that already exists** gets the archive's branches under `refs/remotes/backup/*`, to compare and merge by hand. Its patches are copied to `recovered/`.
- **A missing repo, or an empty folder,** is restored with its uncommitted work, on the branch it was on (or detached, as it was).
- **The workspace folder itself, or a project folder holding nothing but the workspace being restored** (the inside layout), is checked out in place. Any file the archive would replace with different content, tracked or untracked, is first copied to `recovered/<archive>/`.
- **Any other folder that already holds files of its own** is left alone, and the repo is restored into `recovered/<archive>/<name>/repo` instead. A folder such as your home folder is never turned into a repo.
- `.env` files are restored only where missing. Stashes are kept as patches in `recovered/`.
- Claude Code memory and settings are restored only where missing.

Inside a project with the private layout, the pointer files (`CLAUDE.local.md` and the others) are ignored by the project's git and so not in the archive: `bin/roles.sh`, run by bootstrap, rebuilds them.

## Checking it

`bin/doctor.sh` reports the newest scheduled backup's age (from `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/backup.log`, never by listing the backup folder, which can trigger a macOS access prompt), whether the passphrase is in the keychain, and a backup folder in the wrong place. Once a quarter, check that the newest archive really restores:

```sh
cabinet backup --verify      # or bin/backup.sh --verify [folder]
```

It restores the newest archive of this workspace into a temporary folder, as `restore.sh` would, and deletes that copy when it is done (it holds your secrets). For the workspace and each repo it prints one line: restores exactly as it is now, restores with so many files or commits changed since the backup (work done after it), or a problem. A problem is an archive that does not open (a wrong passphrase, or a damaged file), a history that does not rebuild, uncommitted changes that do not apply, files that do not unpack, or a repo that is not in the archive. Any problem makes it exit 1: back up again, then verify that archive. It never touches the workspace, its repos or your settings, and does not check Claude Code's memory or settings. A good result is recorded in `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/backup-verified`, and `bin/doctor.sh` notes when none is recorded or the last is older than 92 days.
