========================================================================

# Troubleshooting

Every message `bin/doctor.sh` can print, what it means and how to fix it. `FIX` lines make the doctor exit 1; `note` lines are information. `<...>` stands for a name, path or number the doctor fills in. Run the doctor again after a fix. The ID names the check: `cabinet doctor --json` gives it with each result, and it stays the same when a message is reworded, so scripts and agents match on the ID, never on the text.

## Product repos

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX <...>: no repo at <...> (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `repos.present` | A repo in `repos.tsv` is not where its row says. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` clones it (it needs a clone URL in the row), or fix the path column. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> missing` | `repos.local-file` | A local-only file listed in `repos.tsv` is not in the repo. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` restores it from `local/<repo>/`. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> not in snapshot (run bin/snapshot.sh)` | `repos.snapshot` | A local-only file has no copy in `local/<repo>/`. | `bin/snapshot.sh`, then commit the workspace. |
| `note <...>/<...> changed since last snapshot` | `repos.snapshot` | A local-only file differs from its copy. | `bin/snapshot.sh` when the change is finished, then commit. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> is tracked in the product repo but listed as local-only` | `repos.local-file-tracked` | The file is committed in the product repo, but `repos.tsv` says it lives outside git there. | Remove it from that repo's git (`git rm --cached`), or from the row's local-only list. |
| `FIX <...>/CLAUDE.md is not a link to AGENTS.md` | `repos.claude-link` | A repo whose row says `yes` to the link has no `CLAUDE.md` link. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` creates it (when the repo has an `AGENTS.md` and no `CLAUDE.md`). |
| `FIX <...>: instruction files show as untracked (missing exclude entry)` | `repos.instructions-excluded` | A repo's local `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` shows in its `git status`. | Add them to that repo's `.git/info/exclude` (keep the entries in `local/<repo>/git-info-exclude`). |
| `repos.tsv: skipped the row named "<...>" (not a plain folder name)` | - | A row's name has spaces or other characters. | Rename it to letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`. |

## Kit and roles

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX kit files edited here (an update will refuse them; move the change to a project file or into the kit): <...>` | `kit.unedited` | A file the kit owns (`CABINET.md`, `bin/`, `.cabinet/`) was changed in the workspace. | Move your change to a project file (`AGENTS.md`, `roles/`, `jobs/`), then `git checkout -- <file>`. |
| `FIX workspace CLAUDE.md link missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `kit.claude-link` | The workspace's `CLAUDE.md` link to `AGENTS.md` is gone. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX HANDOFFS.md missing` | `kit.handoffs-file` | The handoff log was deleted. | Restore it from git. |
| `FIX <...> (run bin/roles.sh)` | `kit.roles` | A built role is missing or out of date (for example after editing `roles/` or `CABINET_ROLES`). | `bin/roles.sh`. |

## Push guardrails

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX git push gate not installed (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.push-gate` | No pre-push hook in the global hooks path. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note repos' own git hooks (pre-commit and others) do not run under the global hooks path: run bin/bootstrap.sh` | `guardrails.hook-passthrough` | The pass-through stubs are missing. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...> sets its own core.hooksPath (<...>), which bypasses the push gate` | `guardrails.repo-hookspath` | A repo sets its own hooks path (husky does), so the global gate is skipped there. | Remove it (`git config --unset core.hooksPath`), or add the gate to that repo's hooks folder yourself. |
| `FIX Claude Code is missing <...> deny rule(s) (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.claude` | `~/.claude/settings.json` lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. If it says the file is not plain JSON, fix the file first. |
| `FIX Codex push rule missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.codex` | Codex does not forbid `git push`. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`; if `~/.codex/rules/default.rules` already exists, add the kit's rules (`.cabinet/guardrails/codex-default.rules`) to it. |
| `FIX agy push deny rule missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.agy` | Antigravity's settings lack the push rule. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Gemini CLI policy missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.gemini` | No `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml`. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Qwen Code is missing <...> deny rule(s) (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.qwen` | `~/.qwen/settings.json` lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Cursor CLI is missing <...> deny rule(s) in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.cursor` | The Cursor CLI's config lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note the Cursor editor keeps its agent's command rules in its own settings, which the kit does not set: only the git push gate applies there` | `guardrails.cursor-editor` | Information: the kit cannot set the editor's rules. | Set its command denylist in the Cursor editor's settings if you want more than the push gate. |
| `FIX Grok does not load the rules in ~/.claude/settings.json (check: grok inspect)` | `guardrails.grok` | Grok is not reading the Claude Code rules (its Claude compatibility may be off). | Turn it on in Grok, or add the rules to `~/.grok/config.toml` by hand. |
| `FIX opencode does not deny: <...> (run bin/bootstrap.sh; a rule in opencode.jsonc comes last and wins)` | `guardrails.opencode` | On opencode 1.x, the resolved rules do not end with the kit's denies. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`; if it still fails, remove the overriding rule from `opencode.jsonc`. |
| `note <...> of opencode cannot be checked from here: confirm its permission settings by hand (the kit's rules are in ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json)` | `guardrails.opencode` | opencode 2.x has no command to print its resolved rules. | Check in opencode that it refuses `git push`. |
| `note <...> is installed and cabinet has no guardrails for it: only the git push gate above applies` | `guardrails.unguarded-tool` | An agent tool the kit does not cover. | Use it for reading and local edits, or add its own deny rules by hand. |
| `FIX scheduled jobs cannot find the runner '<...>' (install it, or fix CABINET_RUNNER / CABINET_RUNNER_CMD, then run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `runner.found` | The runner is not on the PATH scheduled jobs get. | Install it, or fix the setting; then `bin/bootstrap.sh` from a shell where it is on your PATH, so the schedule gets its folder. |
| `FIX scheduled jobs find <...> but not node, which it needs (run bin/bootstrap.sh after installing node)` | `runner.node` | The runner is a Node script and Node is not on the scheduled PATH. | Install Node, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note the custom runner '<...>' has no cabinet guardrails: only the git push gate covers its scheduled runs` | `runner.custom-unguarded` | A custom runner the kit does not know. | Add its own deny rules by hand. |

## Skills and plugins

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note skill '<...>' not installed` | `skills.skill` | A skill in `CABINET_SKILLS` is not in `~/.claude/skills/`. | Install it, or remove it from `CABINET_SKILLS`. |
| `note plugin '<...>' not installed` | `skills.plugin` | A plugin in `CABINET_PLUGINS` is not installed in Claude Code. | Install it, or remove it from `CABINET_PLUGINS`. |

## Guides

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX guides/<...> has no row in the Guides table of AGENTS.md, so agents never read it` | `guides.listed` | A file was added to `guides/` without a row in the "Guides" table. | Add a row: `` `guides/<file>` ``, what it covers, who follows it. See [recipes](recipes.md#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents). |
| `FIX AGENTS.md lists <...>, which does not exist` | `guides.exists` | A row in the "Guides" table names a file that is not in `guides/`. | Restore the file, fix the path, or delete the row. |

## Manual and handoffs

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX OPERATIONS.md does not mention: <...>` | `manual.complete` | The manual has fallen behind a script, job or role. | Add it to `OPERATIONS.md` (`cabinet config --roles` adds role rows for you). |
| `FIX these handoff IDs are used more than once: <...>(file the next free number)` | `handoffs.unique-ids` | Two entries share an ID. | Give the later one the next free number, or mark it with a `- Note: duplicate ID` line. |

## Secrets

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX possible secrets in the workspace's files (remove each and rotate any real key; a false alarm: add not-a-secret to its line): <...>` | `secrets.none` | A line looks like a key, token or password (file and line are named; the value never is). | Remove it, and rotate the key if it was real: it may already be in git history and backups. A false alarm: add `not-a-secret` to its line. |
| `note commits are not checked for secrets: the workspace has no pre-commit hook running bin/secrets.sh (run bin/bootstrap.sh; a hook of your own can call bin/secrets.sh --staged)` | `secrets.hook` | Bootstrap has not run, or the workspace has its own `pre-commit` hook. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`, or call `bin/secrets.sh --staged` from your hook. |

## Uncommitted work

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note the workspace has no commits yet: backups hold its files only (set the owner with cabinet config, then commit)` | `work.no-commits` | Setup did not commit (no owner identity). | `cabinet config --owner "..." --email ...`, then commit the workspace. |
| `note <...> has <...> uncommitted file(s): work in progress, or finished and not committed?` | `work.uncommitted` | A repo has uncommitted changes. | Commit finished work; leave work in progress. |

## Schedules

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX jobs/<...>.job has a WHEN bootstrap cannot schedule ('<...>'): use a time like 7 AM for every day, or days and a time like fri 4 PM or sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM` | `schedules.when` | A mistyped time or day. Bootstrap keeps the working schedule meanwhile. The forms are in [commands](commands.md#schedule-times). | Fix `WHEN`, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> not scheduled (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `schedules.job` | A job has a time but no schedule. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note jobs are not scheduled on this Mac (CABINET_SCHEDULES=off in cabinet.local.env): another Mac runs them; cabinet bootstrap --schedules turns them on` | `schedules.off` | This Mac was set up with `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules`, so the job checks are skipped here. | Nothing, when another Mac runs the jobs. To run them here: `cabinet bootstrap --schedules`. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> runs another workspace: give this one its own slug (cabinet config --slug)` | `schedules.job-owner` | Two workspaces share a slug. | `cabinet config --slug <new>` in one of them. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> is written but not loaded by launchd (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `schedules.job-loaded` | The schedule file exists, but launchd has not loaded it. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...> still runs this workspace under an old name (launchctl bootout gui/\$(id -u)/<...>, then delete <...>)` | `schedules.old-slug` | A schedule left over from an earlier slug. | Run the `launchctl bootout` it names, then delete that file. |

## Backups

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note backups are off on this Mac (cabinet.local.env; cabinet config --this-mac --backup-dir <folder> turns them on)` | `backups.enabled` | This Mac turned backups off for itself (`cabinet config --this-mac --backup-dir off`). | Nothing, when another Mac backs up. To back up here: `cabinet config --this-mac --backup-dir <folder> --apply`. |
| `note backups are off (set CABINET_BACKUP_DIR in cabinet.env, then run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `backups.enabled` | No backup folder set. | `cabinet config --backup-dir <folder>`, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. See [backups](backups.md). |
| `FIX CABINET_BACKUP_DIR must be an absolute path` | `backups.dir-absolute` | A relative backup folder. | `cabinet config --backup-dir <absolute folder>`. |
| `FIX the backup folder is inside <...>: a backup there is lost with it and can be committed (choose a folder outside, then cabinet config)` | `backups.dir-outside` | The backup folder is inside the workspace or one of its repos. | Choose a folder outside them with `cabinet config --backup-dir`. |
| `FIX no scheduled backup in <...>/backup.log yet (launchctl kickstart -k gui/\$(id -u)/<...>.backup)` | `backups.recent` | No scheduled backup has run yet. | Run the `launchctl kickstart` it names, or wait for the time set. |
| `FIX newest backup is <...>h old (<...>): <...>` | `backups.recent` | No scheduled backup in the last 36 hours (the Mac was asleep or the job failed). | Read `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/backup.log`. |
| `note no restore of a backup has been verified on this Mac yet (cabinet backup --verify)` | `backups.verified` | `cabinet backup --verify` has not passed on this Mac. | `cabinet backup --verify` ([backups](backups.md#checking-it)). |
| `note the last verified restore was <...> days ago (<...>): verify again (cabinet backup --verify)` | `backups.verified` | The last good verify is more than 92 days old. | `cabinet backup --verify`. |
| `FIX backup passphrase missing from keychain (<...>, see bin/backup.sh)` | `backups.passphrase` | No keychain item `cabinet.<slug>.backup`. | `security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup -w` (the same passphrase as in your password manager). |

## Other commands

- **`cabinet: not inside a cabinet workspace, or a project with cabinet/ in it`:** a workspace command (`doctor`, `bootstrap`, `brief`, ...) ran outside any workspace. `cd` into the workspace or its project, or start one with `cabinet new` or `cabinet init`.
- **`cabinet: unknown command '<...>'`:** exit 2, with the list of commands.
- **`Not safe to delete: <...>`:** from `cabinet remove`, when the workspace has uncommitted changes or commits on no remote. Commit and push (or copy) that work first; `--force` deletes it anyway.
- **`--fix asks before each step: run it in a terminal, or add --yes`:** `cabinet doctor --fix` had no terminal to ask in.
- **`cabinet: the slug '<...>' is already used by the workspace at <...>`:** choose another with `--slug`. When it says that workspace no longer exists, it lists the steps to free the slug.
- **`cabinet: <...> already has a cabinet workspace: use cabinet update`:** `init` runs once per folder.
- **`cabinet: <...> is inside the repo <...>: run cabinet init at its top folder`:** run it there.
- **`cabinet: these files already exist at paths the kit uses: <...>`:** rename or move those files, then run `cabinet init` again.
- **`<...>: the merge did not produce a valid file (its shape is not what the kit expects), left as is`:** from bootstrap. The file is unchanged; add the kit's rules by hand, or fix the file's shape.
- **An update stops with "edited here, left as is"** or **"already here and not the kit's":** move your change to a project file, restore the kit's file, then `cabinet update` again.


========================================================================
File: core/CABINET.md
========================================================================

# CABINET.md - how this workspace runs

This file comes from the cabinet kit and is replaced on every kit update. Do not edit it here: project rules go in `AGENTS.md`, standing documents (brand, style, policies, business documents) in `guides/` with a row in the "Guides" table of `AGENTS.md`, and project notes for a role in `roles/<role>.md`. A change that should reach every project goes into the kit itself.

Every agent reads this file first, then `AGENTS.md`, then the `AGENTS.md` of the repo it works in, and before any work a guide in `AGENTS.md` covers, that guide. On a conflict the more specific file wins: repo `AGENTS.md` over workspace `AGENTS.md` and its guides over this file. Nothing in a project file or guide may loosen "Never push, merge, publish or release" or "The builder never verifies".

## The workspace

One folder holds the files that tie the project's repos together, and usually the repos themselves; a repo can also live elsewhere (the path column of `repos.tsv`), such as a project the workspace sits beside or inside. The workspace is its own private git repo (except a shared `cabinet/` inside a project, which is part of the project's); each product repo has its own `.git` and is ignored here.

| Path | What it is | Owned by |
|---|---|---|
| `CABINET.md` | This file: how any cabinet workspace runs | the kit |
| `AGENTS.md` (`CLAUDE.md` links to it) | This project: the team, the contracts, the house and product rules | the project |
| `cabinet.env` | Project settings: name, slug, roles, agent tool, backups, layout (the owner and week start are in `AGENTS.md`, the brief time in `jobs/brief.job`) | the project; `cabinet config` changes it |
| `HANDOFFS.md`, `handoffs/` | The one channel between agents, and its closed entries | every agent, by the rules below |
| `BRIEF.md` | The daily brief and the owner's sign-off queue (untracked) | chief-of-staff |
| `OPERATIONS.md` | The owner's manual | the owner, kept current by every agent that changes `bin/`, `jobs/` or the team |
| `agents/`, `.claude/agents/` | The role definitions, generated by `bin/roles.sh` from the kit's roles and `roles/` | generated |
| `roles/<role>.md` | This project's notes for a role, appended to the kit's definition | the project |
| `jobs/<job>.job` | Scheduled agent runs | the project |
| `guides/` | Standing documents every agent follows when its work touches their subject; listed in the "Guides" table of `AGENTS.md` | the owner; agents edit one only when asked |
| `specs/`, `notes/` | Specs, ADRs, verdicts; the owner's notes and decisions | as each role says |
| `repos.tsv` | Every product repo: clone URL, local-only files, `CLAUDE.md` link, and where it lives when not in the workspace | the project |
| `bin/`, `.cabinet/` | Kit scripts, roles, guardrails and schedule templates | the kit |

A workspace can also be a `cabinet/` folder inside a project (`cabinet init --inside`). Then the project's `AGENTS.md` points here, and every path in this file and in the roles is relative to `cabinet/`: run `cabinet/bin/handoffs.sh` from the project's top folder, or work from inside `cabinet/`. The project's repo is the `..` row of `repos.tsv`. When `cabinet.env` says `CABINET_LAYOUT="inside"` and `CABINET_VISIBILITY="private"`, nothing in `cabinet/` ever goes into the project's history; never move its contents into a tracked file of the project.

## Start of every session

1. Read this file, then `AGENTS.md` (its "Guides" table included), then your repo's `AGENTS.md`. Before any work a guide covers, read that guide and follow it.
2. Run `bin/handoffs.sh <your repo or role>`: it prints, in full, every open entry addressed to you. Pick up each one (see "Handoffs").
3. Before changing anything that crosses a repo line, check the contracts table in `AGENTS.md`.
4. If `BRIEF.md` exists, read its line for you.
5. `notes/` holds the owner's decisions and research. Read a note when the owner points to it or your task touches its `topic` or `repos`, and follow its `status` (`draft`, `decided`, `superseded`). Edit notes only when asked.

## Ownership

Each agent owns its repos end to end, documentation included, as the team table in `AGENTS.md` assigns them. No agent writes to a repo it does not own; reading any repo is always fine. A repo with no owning agent is changed only when the owner asks. When your change affects another repo, you file a handoff; you never edit that repo.

## Builders

Product repos are built by builder roles: `backend` (servers, APIs, workers, libraries), `web` (what runs in a browser), `mobile` (iOS and Android apps) and `infrastructure` (CI, deploys, infrastructure as code). The team table in `AGENTS.md` names each repo's owning agent; a repo whose owner is `TBD` gets a builder from `bin/bootstrap.sh` when it first arrives on a Mac, guessed from what the repo holds, and the owner may change the row to another builder, a project role, or `owner`. A builder:

1. **Learns the repo before its first change, and follows it.** The repo's own `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`), `README`, `CONTRIBUTING`, and how it is really built: the package scripts or `Makefile`, the test, lint, type and build commands, the CI configuration, the formatter and lint settings, the folder layout, the dependencies already chosen, and the message style of recent commits. What the repo does wins over the builder's habits and over any default. Never replace its stack, tools or conventions; propose a change as a tier 2 or 3 decision instead. Only a new, empty repo gets defaults: a test command, a linter, a `README` and an `AGENTS.md` that records them, set up first.
2. **Works from a spec or a handoff addressed to it,** and takes nothing else on beyond tier 1 (see "Decision rights and sign-off").
3. **Changes with a test.** A fix starts with a test that fails without it; a feature comes with the tests the repo's style calls for.
4. **Runs the repo's own checks** (tests, lint, types, build) and hands nothing on until they pass. A check that was already failing is named, not hidden.
5. **Commits locally,** in the repo's message style and branch flow, and never pushes, merges, deploys or publishes.
6. **Hands finished work to qa** (and security, and design-lead for anything people see) with `bin/handoff.sh`: what changed, the commits, how to run it, and what to look at. It never verifies its own work. A BLOCK comes back to it as a fix.
7. **Keeps to its repos.** A change another repo needs goes to that repo's owner as a handoff; a contract change follows the contracts table in `AGENTS.md`.

## Handoffs

`HANDOFFS.md` is the one channel between agents. It is durable, so work is never lost when a session ends, and it gives the owner one place to see everything in flight.

- **When your change affects another repo,** file an entry with `bin/handoff.sh --from <you> --to <them> --changed "..." --needed "..." [--depends-on "..."] "<title>"`, which picks the next free ID and commits it (or append one by hand from the template at the top of `HANDOFFS.md`): who it is for, exactly what changed (endpoint, field, limit, status code, default, version, file), what they need to do, and the commit or branch it depends on. Name the entry ID in your summary.
- **When an entry is addressed to you,** verify it against the code before acting: a handoff describes a change, the code is the truth. Set it to `acknowledged` when you start and `done` when your side lands, with the date and your commit. If it is wrong or not needed, set it to `rejected` with the reason.
- **Commit every edit to `HANDOFFS.md` at once,** as its own commit (`handoffs: ...`). If the file holds someone else's uncommitted lines, stage only yours and name the leftovers in your summary; chief-of-staff commits leftovers in its daily run.
- **Only edit entries addressed to you, and only their status lines.** Add a follow-up entry instead of rewriting another. One exception: chief-of-staff may set any entry to `done` when the code shows it landed, and applies the owner's sign-off answers to the entries they name.
- **Dates in an entry's ID and status line are ISO (`2026-10-18`):** a machine format `bin/handoffs.sh` reads to age entries. Prose in an entry uses the house date format.
- **Status lines hold the current state only:** status, date, commit, one sentence. Replace the old state; git keeps the history. A verdict (qa, security, design-lead, architect) is one short line: who, PASS or BLOCK, date, commits, and the path of its note under `specs/qa/`, `specs/security/` or `specs/design/`, written before the line links it.
- **Entries addressed to `owner`** (`founder` means the same person) are decisions or actions only the owner can take.
- **Closed entries leave the file.** chief-of-staff runs `bin/archive-handoffs.sh` daily: it moves every committed `done` or `rejected` entry to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` and commits the move. Archive files are read only. An ID stays unique across all of them (`bin/doctor.sh` checks).

## Decision rights and sign-off

The aim: an organization that runs itself and brings the owner only what needs the owner.

**Functions and leads.** Operations: chief-of-staff. Product: product-manager, with design-lead. Engineering: architect, with the repo agents. Quality and trust: qa, with security. Business: finance. A project enables the roles it needs in `cabinet.env`; a function whose lead is not enabled falls to the owner.

**Three tiers. Every decision belongs to exactly one.**

| Tier | Who decides | What | Logged in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The agent | Reversible, inside its own repo or files, follows existing rules | Commit message or handoff status line |
| 2 | The function lead | Reversible, crosses repos or sets direction for the function, costs nothing | Spec Decisions table (product), ADR (engineering), `specs/design/` (design), qa and security verdicts |
| 3 | Owner sign-off | Irreversible, public, or costs money: push, merge, deploy, publish, release; prices, quotas, plans, coupons, any spend or paid service; the brand guide, logo, positioning, public copy; legal, privacy policy, data retention; adding, changing or removing an agent or its authority | The owner's sign-off queue |

A lead may move a tier 2 question up to the owner when unsure. Nobody moves a tier 3 question down. An agent unsure of the tier treats it as the higher one.

**The sign-off queue.** One place: the top of `BRIEF.md`, kept by chief-of-staff. The owner answers in batches; chief-of-staff applies the answers into the right specs, ADRs and handoffs. Every decision put to the owner, by any agent, has:

- a plain-language question that stands on its own: what it is and why it matters now, with no unexplained item numbers, file names or jargon;
- lettered options, each with its consequence in one line;
- the recommendation of each relevant expert role, each with a one-line reason;
- one overall recommendation;
- whether the decision can be undone.

Keep each item short.

**Silence.** A reversible tier 3 item marked "default" in the queue may go ahead after 72 hours without an objection, but only as far as local commits. Nothing is ever pushed, merged, deployed, published, spent or sent on silence.

**The builder never verifies.** Work is ready for the owner to push only when qa and security have each recorded PASS on its handoff (and design-lead for UI changes, when enabled). A qa or security BLOCK holds the push until fixed; only the owner can override it. A project without qa or security enabled sends that verification to the owner.

## Seats

A seat is an agent or a person; the rules are the same for both.

**Spotting the need.** chief-of-staff owns it; any lead may propose a seat at any time.

- Daily, the brief flags signs that a seat may be needed: recurring work no seat owns; a function falling behind (stale handoffs or a growing backlog for one seat); a planned stage reached; a new product or channel. Evidence only (handoffs, commits, dates), never invented thresholds.
- Monthly, on the first day of the week that `AGENTS.md` names (Monday when it names none) in the first week of the month, a short org review by chief-of-staff with finance: whether every seat still earns its place (keep, change its authority, or retire it), and the gaps from the daily signals.

**Proposal.** Every new seat reaches the owner as one decision in the sign-off queue format: the need, the evidence, agent or person, the cost (from finance, `TBD` until priced), the alternatives (absorb the work into an existing seat, wait, or hire a person), the expert recommendations, and whether it can be undone. If `AGENTS.md` sets an affordability rule, the proposal shows that check. Every seat is the owner's sign-off.

**Onboarding.** The lead the seat reports to owns its onboarding and first month; security sets up and limits its access to what the seat needs; chief-of-staff tracks each new seat through its checklist in the brief until the one-month review.

Agent seat:
1. Definition and limits written: what it owns, decides, escalates and may write.
2. Registered: `roles/<role>.md` (and the role name in `CABINET_ROLES`, then `bin/roles.sh`), the team table in `AGENTS.md`, and `OPERATIONS.md`.
3. Access limited to its own files and repos (security).
4. The push and publish guardrails confirmed for the tool it runs in (`bin/doctor.sh`, "Push guardrails").
5. Trial task, reviewed by its lead.
6. The lead's written corrections recorded into its definition.
7. Review after a month: keep, change or retire.

Person:
1. Contract and accounts as the owner sets them; access set up and limited by security.
2. The push and publish rules below, the brand guide, and the house rules in `AGENTS.md`.
3. Their lead as manager; a first task, reviewed by the lead; the lead's corrections recorded in their role notes.
4. Review after a month: keep, change or retire.

## The owner's manual

`OPERATIONS.md` is how the owner runs everything. Any change to `bin/`, `jobs/`, the roles or the owner's routine updates it in the same commit. `bin/doctor.sh` fails when the manual stops naming a script, job or role.

## Schedule

Agents also run on a local schedule (`bin/scheduled.sh`, one `jobs/<job>.job` each), starting with the daily chief-of-staff brief. Jobs are added as the owner trusts them. `cabinet.env` names the agent tool that runs them (`CABINET_RUNNER`).

## Rules for every repo

- **Never push, merge, publish or release.** Only the owner does. It is enforced in every agent tool cabinet knows (`bin/bootstrap.sh` installs the guardrails for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, opencode and the Cursor CLI; Grok reads the Claude Code rules; the Cursor editor keeps its own settings and has the push gate only): they deny `git push`, `gh pr merge`, `gh release`, write calls through `gh api`, package publishing, reading the GitHub token or the keychain, and the known ways of skipping git hooks as far as each tool's rule format allows (the kit's `docs/guardrails.md` lists the limits per tool); and a global git pre-push hook refuses any push not confirmed at the owner's terminal. Do not try to work around either: a way around them is a reason to stop and ask the owner, never a way to proceed.
- **Local commits are the only git write.** No push, merge, rebase, amend, reset or other history rewrite. A commit that fails review is reverted, or fixed in a follow-up commit; never amended.
- **Commit finished work at once.** Every agent commits its own finished, tested changes locally, each one separately with a clear message in the repo's style, authored and signed as `AGENTS.md` says. Uncommitted changes mean work in progress, and only that; an agent ending a session with uncommitted work says so and why. Commit only your own changes, by pathspec (`git commit -- <paths>`), never someone else's uncommitted work.
- **No fabrication.** Never invent names, limits, prices, dates, library choices or other specifics the owner has not stated or the code does not show. Write TBD, describe the capability, or read the canonical source. When corrected on a fabrication, audit recent work for the same mistake.
- **No secrets in files.** Keys, tokens, passwords and `.env` values never go into a repo, a note, a handoff or a log. The workspace's pre-commit hook (`bin/secrets.sh`) refuses a commit that adds one; never mark a real secret `not-a-secret` to get past it.

## Working in a tool other than Claude Code

Everything here is plain files, so any agent tool, with any model it offers, can run the team. `AGENTS.md` is read by Codex, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode and Cursor, bootstrap sets Gemini CLI to read it, and `CLAUDE.md` links to it for Claude Code. To act as a role, read `agents/<role>.md` and follow it as your instructions. Claude Code also loads the same definitions from `.claude/agents/`.

A tool `bin/doctor.sh` names as having no guardrails is covered only by the git push gate: it could still merge, release or publish. Use it for reading and local edits, or ask the owner before giving it a task that touches GitHub or a package registry.


========================================================================
File: ROADMAP.md
========================================================================

# Roadmap

What cabinet does next, in order. Each item says what is missing today, what it takes, and when it counts as done. Items move to `CHANGELOG.md` when they ship.

**One rule for every item:** cabinet is shaped by the people who use it, not built around one kind of project. It has to fit any product (a web app, a mobile app, a library, a service, client work, a business with little code), any team (one person to a small company, people and agents in any mix) and any experience (new to everything, or expert in some areas). So every item below is optional, turned on and tuned per project in its own settings, and has a sensible default for a project that does not care; nothing assumes a number of repos, a stack, a market, an outside service or a way of working. Where an item needs project-specific detail (what is critical, which contracts exist, what a release is), the project declares it, and the kit supplies the mechanism, not the content.

## 1. Full Linux support

Today cabinet is built and tested on macOS. On Linux the team files, setup and guardrails should work but have never run there, and four parts are macOS only.

- **Schedules:** setup installs, updates and removes systemd user timers (cron where systemd is absent), the same way it handles launchd on macOS. Today setup installs nothing on Linux and says to use cron by hand.
- **Backup passphrase:** read from the Linux secret store (`secret-tool`) or `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE`. The health check accepts either; today it always reports the passphrase missing on Linux.
- **Dates and paths:** the health check computes the backup's age with GNU `date` too (today it uses a macOS-only option), and logs go to `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` on Linux.
- **Tests:** the suite runs on Linux (today it uses the macOS form of `sed -i`), and passes in a Linux container.
- **Install:** `package.json` adds `linux` to `os` (today npm refuses to install on Linux), and the README's platform line says so.

Done when: the full test suite passes on macOS and in a Linux container, and a workspace on Linux runs its brief and backup on schedule with `bin/doctor.sh` all green.

## 2. Windows support, through WSL

Windows runs cabinet through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which gives the Linux support above. Native Windows (PowerShell, or Git Bash, which lacks `jq` and other tools the scripts use) is not a goal.

- A README section: installing WSL, where the workspace should live (the WSL file system, not a mounted Windows drive, for git speed and file permissions), and running the agent tools inside WSL.
- The guardrails for agent tools installed inside WSL; a note on tools installed on the Windows side, which those guardrails do not cover.
- The test suite run under WSL once.

Done when: the full test suite passes under WSL, and the README walks a Windows user from nothing to a working workspace.

## For founders without every skill

The goal: cabinet is equally useful to a founder with no technical or business background and to one who is expert in one area (engineering, design, sales) and lacks the rest, and equally useful for a project that is only an idea and for an established one with code, users, a team and its own ways of working. The team fills what the founder lacks, explains what the founder must decide in the founder's terms, and stays out of the way where the founder is the expert. Today the kit is strong at governance (who decides, independent review, guardrails, the daily sign-off) but assumes the founder knows how to build and run a product. Items marked **pick first** come before the rest. Every item works for both kinds of project: for an established one it learns what is there and follows it, and it never replaces the project's stack, conventions or rules with defaults.

- **The founder's profile.** Ties the items below together. At setup (and with `cabinet config`), the founder says what they know well and what they do not, area by area: engineering, design, product, marketing, finance, legal and admin. Every role reads it: where the founder is expert, agents bring fewer and more technical decisions and skip the explanations; where the founder is new, they explain more, bring the choices pre-made with a recommendation, and say when a professional is needed. Done when: the same decision reaches an expert founder as a short technical choice and a new founder as a plain question with the trade-offs explained, from one profile setting.
- **From an idea to a plan** (pick first). Today the kit starts once a product exists, with `TBD` lines in `AGENTS.md` to fill. A kickoff, run once at setup or any time after, in one of two modes. For a new idea, the product-manager interviews the founder (the problem, who has it, what is in and out of the first version, how success is measured). For an established project, the team first learns what exists (the code, the docs, the git history, the open issues, how it is built, tested and deployed) and asks the founder only what none of that tells. Either way it writes `AGENTS.md`, the specs and a roadmap (for an established project, the current state and what is next), each marked for the founder to confirm. Done when: a founder with only an idea, or with a running product, ends the kickoff with no `TBD` in "What the project is" and "Product rules", and a ranked roadmap that starts from where the project really is.
- **See the result, not only the verdict** (pick first). Today qa records PASS or BLOCK, and a founder who cannot read code approves on trust. Each finished handoff carries evidence the founder can check without code: screenshots, a short recording, a link to try it, or the command output for work with no screen. qa refuses a PASS without it. Done when: every handoff that reaches the founder for sign-off shows what was built.
- **Guard the founder's time and money** (pick first). Today nothing tracks what the agents cost, and the sign-off queue has no limit. AI spend per workspace (what the scheduled runs and sessions cost this week, from what each tool reports), with a budget and a warning before it is passed; and a daily cap on the sign-off queue (for example five decisions, ranked; the rest wait, and the brief says how many), since for a solo founder the queue is the bottleneck. Done when: the founder sees the week's spend and is warned before a budget is passed, and no brief asks more decisions than the cap.
- **Setup without terminal skills.** Today setup needs git, jq and Node.js, quoted options and terms like launchd. One install command that checks every prerequisite and installs what is missing, asking first; messages in plain language, with the technical detail one step away; and `cabinet next` steps that say why each matters. Done when: a founder who has never used a terminal reaches a working workspace by following the screen.
- **Decisions that do not assume expertise.** Today a founder can be asked to pick a database, a host or a payments provider without knowing the trade-offs. Starter stacks, for new projects only: one recommended, well-supported stack for each kind of product, so the first technical choices are made and can be changed later (an established project keeps its stack). And in every technical decision, new or established, what each option costs and what changing it later would take. Done when: a new project's first technical choices arrive made, an established project's stack is never replaced by a starter, and each technical decision shows cost and the cost of changing course.
- **After launch: running, customers and growth.** Today no role covers production or customers. Roles turned on when the product goes live, or at setup for one already live, using what it already has (its hosting, monitoring, support inbox and analytics) before suggesting anything new: reliability (deploys, monitoring, an incident checklist, rollback, a status note for users), support (feedback and support replies, turned into specs) and growth (a landing page, launch posts, finding the first users, and regular posts about the work for founders who build in public, drafted for the owner to approve). Done when: a live product has an owner for incidents, for customers and for growth, each with its checklist.
- **Business basics.** Today nothing tracks the business side a founder without advisors misses: forming a company, a privacy policy and terms, taxes and invoicing, app store rules. A checklist role that tracks these, reminds at the right moment and says when to get a professional; its definition forbids legal or tax advice of its own. Done when: a workspace shows which basics are done, open or need a professional, and the role never gives a legal or tax answer itself.
- **People and agents side by side.** Today every repo or area has an owning agent. An established team has people who own parts of it. Each repo or area is owned by an agent, by a person, or shared: where a person owns it, agents read and propose (a branch, a patch or a handoff with the change) and the person reviews and decides; the team table and the brief say which is which. Done when: no agent changes a person-owned area except by a proposal that person accepts.
- **Work the team's way.** Today agents commit locally and the owner pushes. A team may work through branches, pull requests, required reviews and CI. Agents follow the project's own workflow (branch names, commit style, opening a pull request for review where the team does) while push, merge and release stay with people, as the guardrails already make sure. Done when: in a project that works by pull requests, every agent change arrives as one, and nothing merges without a person.
- **The existing backlog** (needs the owner's decision first: it reads an outside service). An established project's open issues and roadmap live in its tracker. A one-time import, then a regular read, turns them into specs and handoffs with links back, without changing the tracker. Done when: the team's open work appears in the workspace, each item linked to its source, and nothing is written to the tracker.
- **Learn by example.** Today the templates show the format, full of `TBD`. A filled example workspace for a made-up product (a finished `AGENTS.md`, real-looking handoffs, a brief with its sign-off queue, a spec, a guide), shipped in the docs and kept in step with the templates by the tests. Done when: every template file has a filled counterpart in the example, and the tests fail when they drift apart.

## Running the work

Patterns proven in daily use of an agent team, made general. Each is optional and declared by the project; items marked **pick first** come before the rest.

- **A pipeline runner** (pick first). Today the owner or chief-of-staff starts each next agent by hand, which is the bottleneck for a founder without people. A runner moves one piece of work through the steps the project already has (spec ready, the owning agent builds, the reviewers the project enabled verify, fixes after a BLOCK, a re-check) and stops when the work is ready for the owner to push; tiers and sign-off do not change, and the runner decides nothing itself. The project sets which steps apply, how many times a repeated BLOCK is retried before it stops and asks, and whether it runs on demand or on a schedule. Adding it changes what runs unattended, so turning it on is the owner's decision. Done when: a ready spec reaches "ready to push" with no agent started by hand, and stops to ask after the set number of BLOCKs.
- **Stricter checks for what must not break** (pick first). Today `AGENTS.md` has one `TBD` line for "what needs a stricter gate". The project declares its critical areas, whatever they are for it (payments, data import, anything with personal data, a public API, a release to an app store), and for each: the extra verdicts required, the evidence required (for example replaying a saved set of real inputs and comparing every result, or a load test), and, for an area that calls an outside service, a request budget that a change may not raise without the owner. qa refuses a PASS without them, and the brief shows which pending work touches a critical area. Done when: a change in a declared area cannot reach "ready to push" without its declared verdicts and evidence.
- **A capability inventory** (pick first). Today nothing records what the product can actually do. A living list, read from the code (and from the docs for a product with little code): every capability, its status (live, built but not released, behind a flag, planned), where it lives, and what it depends on, re-checked against the code by an agent and verified by qa. It is the base for the roadmap, pricing and plans, and the first thing the kickoff writes for an established project. Done when: every capability the code has is in the list, and a re-check reports any that were added, changed or removed.
- **Push deploys, said plainly** (pick first). Today nothing marks a repo where pushing goes live. A column in `repos.tsv` says what a push does (nothing, deploys a preview, deploys to production, publishes a release), and the brief, the digest and the sign-off queue say so beside every push the owner is asked for: "pushing this goes live". Done when: every push request for a repo marked as deploying says it is a live deploy.
- **Checks on contracts between repos.** Today the contracts table names each contract and its source of truth, and nothing verifies them. A contract can name its check (a script, a schema comparison, a test), run by the doctor and by qa before a push; a change on one side that breaks the other is caught then, not by users. Done when: a declared contract with a check fails the review of a change that breaks it.
- **One writer for shared outputs.** Today two agents can work in the same repo copy and collide. A project can name a repo or area with a single writer (a docs site, a website, a release): the others write their part in their own repos and hand it off, and only the writer commits there. Done when: in a single-writer area, every commit comes from its writer, and the others' content arrives through handoffs.
- **Names for the team, and an org page.** Today roles are named by their file (`product-manager`). A project can give each role a title and a display name (for example "Head of Product"), used wherever decisions name each expert's recommendation; and a page generated from the roles and the team table shows who owns what, decides what and reports to whom, for the founder, for people joining, or for a public team page the owner approves. Done when: every decision in the queue names its experts by their titles, and the page rebuilds from the roles on every change.
- **A market watch job.** Today nothing keeps an eye on the market. An optional weekly job tracks what the project names: other products, prices, launches, reviews, rules in its industry, and reports what changed since last week, for the team only. Done when: a project that turns it on gets a weekly report of changes, and nothing from it reaches anything published.
- **A readable manual.** Today the owner's manual is Markdown. It is also built as a formatted page (contents, links, search), rebuilt whenever `OPERATIONS.md` changes, and the doctor says when the page is behind. Done when: the page always matches the Markdown.

## Ideas to pick from

Not ranked yet; each is picked and ordered when its implementation starts.

### The daily loop

- **Answer from the digest.** Today `cabinet digest` gathers every sign-off queue, but each answer still means going into that workspace. `cabinet answer <workspace> "1: approve; 2: no"` delivers the answers to that workspace, where its chief-of-staff applies them on its next run, as if given there. Done when: answers given from anywhere reach the right workspace once, are applied there, and the next digest no longer lists them.
- **A decisions log.** Today the owner's answers are applied into specs and handoffs, so "what did I decide about X, and when" means searching several files. Each answer is recorded with its date, the question and the outcome in one file per workspace, and `cabinet decisions [word]` searches it. Done when: every applied answer has its entry, and a search by word finds it.
- **A weekly review job.** Today the daily brief looks at today. An optional job, on the day the week starts, sums up the week: what shipped, which handoffs closed, which decisions were made, what is stuck and for how long, and how that compares with the week before. Done when: a workspace can turn it on in setup or config, and it runs on the week's first day.
- **Run history and failure alerts.** Today a failed scheduled run shows only as a late brief the next day. `cabinet runs` lists each job's recent runs (when, how long, success or failure, from the job logs), and a failed scheduled run, or one stopped by its time limit, can send a notification and is named in the next brief. Done when: a failing job is reported the same morning, and `cabinet runs` shows its last runs.

### Control

- **Pause and resume.** Today stopping the schedules for a holiday, a trip or a project on hold means turning them off one by one and setting them up again. `cabinet pause [until <date>]` stops every schedule of one workspace, or of all of them with `--all`, and `cabinet resume` (or the date passing) brings them back exactly as they were; `cabinet list`, the digest and the doctor show a paused workspace as paused, not broken. Done when: pause and resume leave every schedule as it was, and a pause with a date ends on its own.
- **Guardrails status and removal.** Today the guardrails are checked per workspace by the doctor, and removed by hand from each tool's settings. `cabinet guardrails` shows, for every agent tool on the Mac, which of the kit's rules are in place, and `cabinet guardrails remove` takes out exactly what cabinet added (from the backups bootstrap made, or rule by rule), leaving the owner's own rules. Done when: after `remove`, each tool's settings match what they were before the first bootstrap, apart from the owner's later changes.

### Starting and working

- **Choose the model, and check it exists.** Today cabinet chooses only the agent tool (`CABINET_RUNNER`); every scheduled job runs with that tool's default model, and the only way to name a model is a custom runner command, which nothing checks and which loses what the built-in runners pass (such as the named role). A `--model` setting for the workspace (`CABINET_MODEL`) and an optional `MODEL=` per job file (one model for the brief, another for heavier jobs), passed through each tool's own model option. The check: where a tool can list its models without a paid call, setup, config and `cabinet doctor` confirm the model is there; where it cannot, an explicit opt-in check makes one short real call, since that costs a little. Each tool's model option and listing command is confirmed live before the kit relies on it, as the Cursor rules were. Done when: a mistyped model is caught before the first scheduled run in every tool that can tell, and the docs say for each tool which kind of check it gets.

- **`cabinet start <role>`.** Today a session as a role is set up by hand in the agent tool. `cabinet start qa` opens the configured agent tool in the workspace with that role's definition and its open handoffs loaded, for every tool cabinet supports. Done when: one command starts a working session as any enabled role, in each supported tool.
- **Presets for kinds of project.** Today every new workspace starts from the same templates, with many `TBD` lines. `cabinet new --preset <kind>` (for example a web product, a mobile app, a library, client work) adds starter product rules, guides, roles and jobs that fit. Done when: a preset leaves fewer `TBD` lines than plain setup, and a project can still change everything it added.
- **Adopt an existing agent setup.** Today a workspace built by hand (its own `AGENTS.md`, handoff log, role definitions, notes) can only be rebuilt from scratch. `cabinet adopt` maps what it finds onto cabinet's files, keeping the content and history, and lists what it could not map. Done when: a hand-built workspace becomes a cabinet workspace without losing a file, and `cabinet doctor` passes on it.

### Teams

- **A shared library of roles and guides.** Today a role or guide written for one project is copied by hand into the next. `cabinet add role <git url | workspace>` (and `cabinet add guide`) installs it, records where it came from, and updates it the way the kit updates, never over a local edit. Done when: a team keeps one copy of a role or guide and every project that uses it can take its updates.
- **`cabinet update --dry-run`.** Today an update applies at once and stops only on an edited kit file. The dry run lists every kit file the update would change, with the diff, and the changelog it would show, and writes nothing. Done when: the dry run predicts exactly what the update then does.

### Needing the owner's decision first

These send data out of the machine or depend on outside services, so each starts as a decision for the owner.

- **Digest notifications by email, Slack or Telegram**, for owners away from the Mac.
- **A CI check for shared workspaces**, verifying the handoff log, the built roles and the guides table on every pull request.

## Later, when a project needs it

- **Hardening found in review:** archives use AES-256-CBC without a MAC (tampering shows only as a tar or gzip error); the keychain item can be read without a prompt by any process of the user (deny rules stop agents in the guarded tools; creating the item to always ask would need a decision for scheduled backups); opencode agent-level and project-level configs, and Qwen workspace settings, can loosen the global rules (`bin/doctor.sh` checks only the global result); folder names without Latin letters or digits need `--slug`; on opencode 2.x, `bin/doctor.sh` cannot read the resolved permission rules (its debug commands need opencode's background service), so its guardrails are unverified there.

- **More than one owner:** today the kit assumes one person signs off. Two founders, or a lead per area, each sign off their own decisions: owners named in `AGENTS.md` with what each decides, every sign-off item addressed to one of them, the brief's queue grouped by owner, and the digest showing each person only their own. The push gate and guardrails stay per person. Wait until a team needs it: it is the largest change here. Done when: an item addressed to one owner reaches only that owner, and an owner's answer applies only to their items.
- **One Mac runs the jobs, without asking teammates:** in a shared workspace, a teammate must remember `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules`, or their Mac schedules the brief too and the team gets two. A choice to study: record in the shared `cabinet.env` which Mac runs the jobs (filled at setup with the owner's Mac), so bootstrap on any other Mac skips schedules on its own and names the Mac that runs them, while `--schedules` still lets a Mac take over. Open questions: how to tell Macs apart (the computer name changes when a Mac is renamed, which would stop its schedules until re-recorded), what the doctor reports on each side, and how a handover works when the owner's Mac is gone. Done when: a teammate who clones a shared workspace and runs a plain `cabinet bootstrap` schedules nothing, and the owner's Mac keeps its schedules.
- **Projects in other languages:** `cabinet init` reads `pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod` and `composer.json` for the name, description and test commands, as it reads `package.json` today.
- **Install without Node.js:** `git clone` and one symlink, with the version pin kept as a git tag in `cabinet/.cabinet/` and read by `cabinet update`. The npm package stays the main route.


========================================================================
File: CHANGELOG.md
========================================================================

# Changelog

Each version says what changed and anything a workspace must do by hand after `npx cabinet update`, which prints these entries.

## 0.1.0 - Unreleased

First version.

### Setup and settings

- Installed per workspace as the dev dependency `@tarekraafat/cabinet`; the package names its repository, home page and issue tracker on GitHub, publishes as public, and installs on macOS only until Linux support ships.
- `cabinet new` asks its setup questions in a terminal (name, folder, owner, roles, agent tool, brief time, week start, backups, repos); each is also an option, and `--yes` skips them for scripts.
- `cabinet init` adds cabinet to an existing project: inside it as `cabinet/`, private or shared, or beside it; or makes an existing folder of repos the workspace. Nothing existing is replaced. It fills the project name, description, test commands, repository URL and owner from the project's `package.json` and git, each marked with its source.
- `cabinet config` changes settings after setup: the same questions with the current answers as defaults. It keeps the team tables, roles and schedules in step, and moves schedules on a slug change. `cabinet config --this-mac --backup-dir <folder>|off [--backup-time <time>]` sets backups for one Mac only, in `cabinet.local.env`, so each teammate in a shared workspace picks their own folder or none; `--clear` follows `cabinet.env` again.
- `cabinet update` applies the installed kit and shows the changelog since the workspace's version; `cabinet changelog`, `status`, `version` and `outdated`.
- `cabinet remove` removes a workspace (its schedules, logs and folder, and inside a project what setup added), refusing work that exists nowhere else unless `--force`.
- `--dry-run` for `new`, `init` and `config`. `repos.tsv` takes an optional path column for a repo that lives outside the workspace.

### The team

- Core rules (`CABINET.md`): workspace layout, handoffs, three decision tiers, the sign-off queue, silence, the builder never verifies, seats and onboarding, git and release rules.
- Roles: chief-of-staff, product-manager, architect, qa, security, design-lead, finance. Project notes and project-only roles through `roles/`.
- Builders: `backend`, `web`, `mobile` and `infrastructure` write the product's code. Each is built when it owns a repo in the team table of `AGENTS.md`; `bin/bootstrap.sh` gives a repo whose owner is `TBD` the builder it most looks like when the repo first arrives. A builder learns how its repo is already built and follows it, tests every change, commits locally and hands finished work to qa (`CABINET.md`, "Builders").
- `guides/` for the project's standing documents (brand, style, policies, business documents), listed in a "Guides" table in `AGENTS.md` that every agent reads; `CABINET.md` ranks guides with `AGENTS.md`, and `bin/doctor.sh` reports a guide with no row and a row with no file. A recipe and a concepts section say where each kind of rule goes and which wins.

### Commands

- One command for everything: `cabinet doctor`, `bootstrap`, `brief`, `run <job>`, `handoffs`, `handoff`, `archive`, `roles`, `backup`, `restore`, `snapshot` and `move` run the workspace's scripts (handoffs, handoff, archive-handoffs, roles, scheduled, bootstrap, doctor, snapshot, backup, restore, move) from any folder inside the workspace or its project. `cabinet next` says what to do next.
- `cabinet handoff --from <name> --to <name> --changed "..." --needed "..." "<title>"` (`bin/handoff.sh`, which `CABINET.md` tells agents to use) files a handoff with the next free ID for today, today's date and the template's lines, and commits it on its own; with someone else's uncommitted lines in `HANDOFFS.md`, it writes the entry but does not commit, so their lines never go into its commit.
- `cabinet digest`: one morning read with the sign-off queue and the owner's actions from the latest brief of every workspace on this Mac. `--write <file>` writes it to a file, `--notify` sends a macOS notification with the counts, and `--schedule [<when>]` (default every day at 10:00 AM; or another time, or chosen days and a time; `off` to stop) runs it as one launchd job for the whole Mac. The chief-of-staff role writes the brief's parts under fixed `## ` headings so the digest can find them.
- `cabinet list`: every workspace on this Mac in one table (kit version, what waits on the owner, the doctor's count, the latest brief).
- `bin/doctor.sh` leads with a summary of what needs attention, and `--fix` runs the fixes it knows (asking first).
- One command table in `bin/cabinet` drives `cabinet help`, `cabinet <command> --help`, `cabinet help --json` (every command and option, for agents) and tab completion (`cabinet completion bash|zsh`: commands, options, and job names for `cabinet run`).
- JSON for agents and scripts: `--json` for `status`, `doctor`, `next`, `handoffs [name]`, `digest` and `list`; every doctor result carries a stable check ID, listed in the troubleshooting docs.
- Dates people read (backup age, brief time, restore) are written as `18 Oct 2026, 2:30 PM`.

### Schedules

- Jobs as `jobs/<job>.job`, scheduled daily or weekly by launchd. A run is stopped, with everything it started, after its time limit: `TIMEOUT` minutes in the job file, else `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT` in `cabinet.env` (default 60; `0` for none), with the reason in the job's log. `bin/bootstrap.sh` adds, updates or removes each schedule to match `jobs/` and the backup setting.
- One form for every schedule (the brief, any job, the backup time, the digest): 12-hour times (`7 AM`, `4:30 PM`), every day or on days, one or several (`fri 4 PM`, `sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM`), with days by short or full name in any case. Times are stored and shown as `4:00 PM`; 24-hour times are still read.
- Scheduled runners: claude, codex, gemini, qwen, grok, opencode, cursor, and `custom` for any other tool (`CABINET_RUNNER_CMD`).
- `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules` (and `--schedules` to undo it): a Mac that should not run the workspace's jobs, such as a teammate's in a shared workspace, skips their schedules from then on; the choice is saved in `cabinet.local.env`, which git never tracks.

### Guardrails and safety

- Guardrails for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, opencode and the Cursor CLI (Grok reads the Claude Code rules; the Cursor rule shapes were probed live on Cursor CLI 2026.10.16), checked by `bin/doctor.sh` (opencode on 1.x only), which also names installed tools it cannot guard; and the owner's pre-push gate for every tool.
- Values from a cloned project's `package.json` never reach a shell (only plain values are used, the description is quoted as data); clone URLs and repo names are checked; a slug another workspace uses is refused.
- Backups must live outside the workspace and its repos, clean up only their own archives, and restore never loses a file. `cabinet backup --verify` restores the newest archive into a temporary folder, checks the workspace and each repo against it (a damaged or incomplete archive fails), and deletes the copy; the doctor notes when no restore has been verified in 92 days (`backups.verified`).
- Config files keep their permissions and symlinks, and a file that is not plain JSON is left alone; every git hook passes through to the repo's own under the global hooks path.
- A secrets check: `cabinet secrets` (`bin/secrets.sh`) looks for keys, tokens and passwords in the workspace's files and names each file and line, never the value; the doctor runs it (`secrets.none`), bootstrap places a pre-commit hook in the workspace that refuses a commit adding one (`secrets.hook`), and `not-a-secret` on a line marks a false alarm.

### Docs

- For people: a short README with a quick start, the daily loop and a glossary; a tutorial for the first day and a recipes page for common tasks; `docs/` with the full command reference, layouts, concepts, guardrails, backups and every doctor message.
- For agents: `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` with every page in one file, and `AGENTS.md` for working on the kit.
- The tests fail when the docs fall behind the code, a link or heading anchor is broken, `llms-full.txt` is stale, or the README's clone command does not match the repository in `package.json`.


========================================================================
File: AGENTS.md
========================================================================

# AGENTS.md - working on the cabinet kit

Read this before changing anything in this repository. It is for agents (and people) improving the kit itself. The rules agents follow inside a workspace made by the kit are in `core/CABINET.md`, which becomes each workspace's `CABINET.md`.

## What is where

| Path | What it is | Ends up in a workspace as |
|---|---|---|
| `bin/cabinet` | The `cabinet` command: setup, settings, removal, updates, and every workspace script as a command run from anywhere inside the workspace | (runs from the installed package) |
| `scripts/*.sh` | The workspace scripts; `lib.sh` is shared and sourced by the rest, and `when.sh` is the one parser for schedule times, sourced by `lib.sh` and by `bin/cabinet` | `bin/*.sh` |
| `core/CABINET.md` | How a workspace runs: handoffs, tiers, sign-off, seats, git rules | `CABINET.md` |
| `roles/*.md` | The kit's roles | `.cabinet/roles/`, built into `agents/` and `.claude/agents/` |
| `guardrails/` | Deny rules for each agent tool, the push gate, the hook pass-through stub | `.cabinet/guardrails/`, installed machine-wide by bootstrap |
| `launchd/job.plist` | The schedule template | `.cabinet/launchd/` |
| `templates/workspace/` | Project files placed once by `new` and `init` | the workspace's own files |
| `docs/`, `README.md`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` | Documentation, shipped in the npm package. `llms-full.txt` is built from the pages `llms.txt` lists | (not copied) |
| `tools/build-llms-full.py` | Builds `llms-full.txt` (`npm run docs`; not shipped) | |
| `test/smoke.sh` | The whole test suite (not shipped) | |

Kit files are replaced on every `cabinet update` and must never be edited in a workspace; project files are the project's own after setup.

## Rules

1. **Never touch the real machine while testing.** Every test and experiment runs in a `mktemp -d` folder with `HOME` pointed inside it (git then reads that folder's `.gitconfig` as its global config), and a fake `launchctl` first on `PATH` from the very start, never added only by a later step. Never read or write the real `~/.claude`, `~/.qwen`, `~/.cursor`, `~/.config`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, the keychain or the global git config. `test/smoke.sh` does this in its header for every section; follow its pattern. After an experiment, check that `launchctl list` shows no `ai.cabinet.` job you did not mean to load.
2. **Never weaken a guardrail, and never test one by trying a real push, merge or publish.** Test a rule with the tool's own matcher, or with a harmless command of the same shape (for example `git log` for `git push`). A new rule format is untested until shown to work, and the docs say so.
3. **bash 3.2.** macOS ships it, so the kit runs on it: no `mapfile`, no associative arrays, no `${var,,}`; guard empty arrays (`${a[@]+"${a[@]}"}`); declare an array on its own `local` line; no apostrophe inside `${x:+...}` in double quotes.
4. **Untrusted values never reach a shell.** Anything from a cloned project (`package.json`, folder names, git remotes) is checked (`safe`, `url_ok`, `name_ok` in `bin/cabinet`) before it is written into `cabinet.env`, `repos.tsv` or a schedule. `cabinet.env` and job files are sourced as shell.
5. **Never lose a user's data.** A config file is changed only through `write_into` (written only when the result is valid and non-empty); an existing file is kept, never replaced; restore copies anything it would replace to `recovered/` first.
6. **Docs match the code.** A change to a command, option, file, message or behavior updates `docs/` (and `README.md` when it is user-facing) in the same change, then `npm run docs` rebuilds `llms-full.txt`. `npm test` fails when a command, option, script, doctor message or check ID is missing from the docs, a link or heading anchor is broken, or `llms-full.txt` is stale.
7. **One command table.** Every `cabinet` command and option is a row in `commands_table` in `bin/cabinet`; help, `--help`, `help --json` and tab completion are made from it. A new command or option starts there, then its parser and dispatcher line; the tests fail when the three disagree.
8. **Stable IDs for machines.** Each doctor check has an ID (`ok <id> "message"`), and each `cabinet next` step has one. A new check gets a new ID, listed in `docs/troubleshooting.md`; an ID or a JSON field is never renamed or removed without a changelog entry that says so.
9. **Every change has a test** in `test/smoke.sh`, and an entry in `CHANGELOG.md` under the next version.
10. **Writing.** ASCII punctuation only (no em or en dashes, no curly quotes). Dates people read as `18 Oct 2026`; machine formats stay ISO. No personal or project names, local paths, or comparisons with other products. Name third-party tools only as facts (which tools have guardrails).
11. **Never push, merge, publish or release.** Only the maintainer does. Commit finished, tested work locally, with no AI or tool attribution lines.

## Checks

```sh
npm test                                      # every section, about a minute; must end with PASS
npm test -- init config                       # only the sections whose name has a word, and what they need
CABINET_PRIVATE_WORDS="word1 word2" npm test  # also fails on any private word in the kit
npm run docs                                  # rebuild llms-full.txt after changing a doc
npm pack --dry-run                            # what the package ships
```

A new test section is a `section "<name>" "<numbers of the sections it needs>"` line and an `sN()` function in `test/smoke.sh`, ending with `return 0`. Before finishing, run each section you touched alone (`npm test -- "<its name>"`): that proves its list of needs is complete.
